speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for weeks Canadians have been led to expect a federal budget filled with significant measures to address the mounting number of casualties from the Toiy voyage to the bottom of the economy.
The document received Monday will be remembered as an April fool's budget, a sad hoax with nothing new and nothing now. This budget is more a prophecy than a plan. Virtually no new measures are included for 1993-94, nor is any improvement in unemployment or the deficit promised for the coming year.
Rather than assist growth this government assumes growth and assumes that Canadians will wait until 1998 for new jobs. Each Canadian who is out of work needs a new job, not the snow job offered by this government.
Canadians are tired of a regime that finds ways to be more mean with less means.

Mr. Speaker, in the budget that was presented by the Minister of Finance on Monday there were provisions for the privatization of a number of Crown corporations and other bodies. Among these was a commitment to study the feasibility of privatizing Transport Canada's helicopter operations.
Transport Canada operates a fleet of 44 helicopters whose chief responsibilities are navigational aid calibration, resupply operations, aviation inspector training, ice reconnaissance and pollution control.
Many of these responsibilities of Transport Canada's helicopter fleet are critical to save marine operations off the coastlines of Canada, including the Bay of Fundy which is partially in my riding of Fundy-Royal.
I would urge the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance to ensure that fiscal responsibility does not take precedence over the safety of mariners because no price is too great when human lives are at risk.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the President of the Treasury Board announced the government's plans to cut at least 16,500 jobs in the federal Public Service over the next five years and to review its work force adjustment policy. These measures are an obvious attempt by the Conservatives to blame public servants for their own incompetence in managing the economy.

According to Treasury Board officials these cuts could mean a loss of $825 million to the national capital region's economy. If it is wise management the government wants, why is it not listening to the public accounts committee and the Auditor General's recommendations instead of cutting services that are provided to Canadians?
What Canada needs is not more unemployment or more people on welfare. What it needs to get the economy moving again is jobs, jobs and jobs.
April 28, 1993

Mr. Speaker, on a sombre note I rise to pay tribute to victims of work related accidents on this National Day of Mourning.
In Canada work place fatalities and injuries cost about $9 billion each year for direct compensation to individuals, retraining and lost productivity.
No amount of dollars can replace a human life. Occupational health and safety is everyone's concern. Safety and health efforts must be both preventive and proactive.
Education and training are required to nurture the kind of awareness that will minimize work place accidents and illnesses. While governments and laws serve a useful regulatory function, it is still the workers and employers who must work together to create safe work places.
On this sombre occasion, it is not enough to mourn those who have died. We must encourage everyone, labour or management, to rededicate themselves to improved safety programs and to making safe and healthy work environments a reality.

Mr. Speaker, the bond rating agencies and the national media claim that this government has not made enough cuts.
That depends on who people are and where they live. Young people in Prince Albert-Churchill River and other far away places in this country will pay for the deficit with their futures.
Their futures depend on training, experience and research and development but my riding alone will lose over $1.5 million in training funding because of the effect of UI changes on the CJS program.
The government put control over student loans in the hands of the Royal and Commerce banks. Students who do not have a local branch or come from low-income families can go to the end of the line.
As MPs we all know the government cut the SEED program, which means fewer summer jobs. It cut funding for friendship centres which provide support for aboriginal youth. It cut federal-provincial forestry and mining agreements which are the only source of research and development in my constituency.
Shame on the government for making young people pay for the deficit with their futures, and shame on the national media for not reporting what is really going on this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to mention the impact of the budget on transfer payments to the provinces.
The message from the Minister of Finance is that it would be irresponsible to penalize the provinces by reducing transfer payments at a time when they already have trouble making ends meet.
In fact, our government has decided to act responsibly by urging the provinces to join us in seeking concrete solutions to the debt problem.
There is only one taxpayer, and the only way to deal with our tax problems is to cut spending on government operations, be better managers, in co-operation with the province, and reduce the tax burden on Canadian taxpayers.

We must secure the integrity of our country first.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make it clear at the outset that I speak as a private member and not as the labour critic for the Liberal Party.
We are now in the process of revamping the Canada Labour Code. Among the suggestions I make to the House is one which would affect workers when they reach the final bargaining stage of a given work conflict.
April 28, 1993

I urge the House to consider the interest of the employees in allowing the employees to have a say in their future through a vote on an offer made by the management.
This is a feature which is already built into the constitutions of some unions but not all of them, which means that in some cases a significant number of employees may want to vote on the offer.
This feature might be of particular benefit when work conflicts last for an inordinate length of time. It should be noted that three provincial NDP governments, in Ontario, B.C. and Saskatchewan, already have this as part of their labour laws.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to applaud the government of the province of Alberta for its initiatives to get people off welfare and into the labour market.
In 1990 the province began its Supports for Independence Program. The pilot projects have been a success and the minister of family and social services has announced a three-year plan to channel resources to provide support and incentive so that people on welfare complete their schooling, acquire job skills and find work.
Costs are recovered through a redistribution of welfare dollars. The focus has shifted from simply covering immediate financial needs to looking at the needs of each individual in order to get back on his or her feet.
It is a positive effort with the long-term goal of providing a path for people on welfare to a future of economic self-sufficiency. It is working because many on welfare want to be self-reliant.
This initiative is one that the federal government should encourage all provinces to follow.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents have been phoning my office with a very serious question. Namely, with one million children living in poverty and 1.4 million unemployed how can the
Prime Minister proceed with a $1 million farewell tour of Europe?
This leaves a bitter taste in the mouths of those who live hand to mouth, and further betrays the taxpayers who will be footing the bill for this extravaganza. These Canadians can never dream of spending thousands a night for hotel rooms for themselves and hangers-on. Many count themselves lucky to have a roof above them and a pillow on which to lay their heads.
A word of advice to this government on investing. Take the $1 million and send it to food banks like Winnipeg Harvest. For every $1 donated $20 worth of food can be gathered and distributed. Or take the money and put it into job training for the unemployed. That is investing in the future of all Canadians, not just in the future of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, those who criticize the federal government's intention to buy EH-101 helicopters never acknowledge the positive impact of this purchase.
The cost of the helicopters is projected to be $4.4 billion in 1988 dollars with a positive impact to the Canadian aviation industry in the amount of $3.2 billion. The contract would be spread out over 13 years and have a continuous benefit to all of Canada.
Recently an aerospace industry in Nova Scotia was forced to lay off workers and in its press release stated that the lay-off would not be necessary if it had the projected work from the EH-101 helicopter contract. In fact, instead of lay-offs it would be hiring more people for long-term, quality jobs.
To those who question the price of the helicopters I say that they must also consider the tremendous positive impact. To purchase a lower quality helicopter with no benefit to the Canadian industry would be worse than to buy a more expensive EH-101 when there is such a significant impact on our economy.

Mr. Speaker, today, April 28, is Canada's National Day of Mourning for workers killed and injured on the job. It

April 28, 1993
Oral Questions
marks the third such official memorial since my NDP colleague, the hon. member for Churchill, succeeded in persuading Parliament to officially recognize this important day of reflection and commitment.
On this day thousands of Canadian workers and others have gathered in hundreds of communities across Canada to remember the approximately 1,000 of their workmates who have died in the work place during this past year and the roughly one million who have been injured on the job.
We particularly remember the 26 miners who were killed suddenly in the Westray coal mine explosion of May 9, 1992 and the nine who died at the Giant Yellowknife mine. However, it is not enough to remember.
Let us commit ourselves to improving the safety, health and related legislation which protects those who produce and distribute our wealth.
In particular, I urge this government to proclaim immediately the health and safety part III of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act which this House passed in 1986 and to enact Criminal Code amendments to protect Canadian loggers and mill workers from those who would seriously endanger their lives by the spiking of trees.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House on this third day of National Consumer Week to highlight the importance of consumers in our marketplace.
Under the theme "It's Everybody's Business" National Consumer Week intends to heighten public awareness of consumer and marketplace issues. Every day millions of Canadians all across the country step into the national marketplace to choose from a sophisticated array of goods and services.
Individually, consumers might feel that their purchases have little impact on the businesses that serve them and less effect on the economy. Collectively however their decisions have an enormous effect on Canada's national economy and its ability to sustain itself against increasing competition.
That is why competent, well-informed and demanding consumers are a vital link in the chain that leads to prosperity. National Consumer Week is an invitation to all Canadians to work together in order to maintain a fair and efficient marketplace.
National Consumer Week will provide Canadians with an opportunity to become better informed on marketplace issues that concern them as well as their own rights and responsibilities in the marketplace.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
The minister has been trying to make excuses for the market's negative reaction to the incompetence and mismanagement shown by him and the Conservatives when it comes to the handling of Canada's financial affairs. Speaking about his budget he said: "I think there were hyped up expectations-I guess there is disappointment in that regard". Disappointment is an understatement.
Why is the minister blaming others for this sorry state of affairs? Did he not create these hyped up expectations himself? Why did he do this if he was not able to follow through in his budget both on the deficit and with a strategy for strong job creation and growth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the December statement and the budget were dedicated to creating the environment for economic growth and the creation of jobs while at the same time dealing with the fiscal problems of the nation. They also set in place a process to deal with the deficit problems faced not only by the federal government but by the provincial governments as well.
If the hon. member were to recall the position of the business community on the budget back in 1985, it criticized that budget when we were going to take $13.8 billion worth of expenditure cuts over a five-year period. It found that budget to be too tough, too mean-spirited and withdrew support for it.
April 28, 1993

It is that same business community that today is saying we did not go far enough when we are providing for expenditure cuts of $30.7 billion over a five-year period.

Mr. Speaker, are we seeing the end of a love affair between the Conservatives and business?
The Minister of Finance has also been reported as excusing himself and the Conservatives for the mismanagement and incompetence I have spoken about when it comes to handling Canada's financial affairs as shown by his budget because of the leadership race and the forthcoming general election.
I ask the minister why in his budget did the political well-being of the Conservative Party turn out to be more important than the economic well-being of Canada and the need both for the right action when it came to fiscal management and a strategy for strong job creation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, clearly the well-being of Canada, Canadians and the Canadian economy was on my mind when I put this budget together. That is why, despite the resistance of the opposition who have refused to support the expenditure reduction initiatives, every single one of them since we have been in office, we continue to move forward.
The budget sets out to achieve the deficit targets for 1993-94. It provides zero growth in public expenditures. That is the lowest rate of growth in 40 years, since 1952. Program spending will come down to a 13.9 per cent share of the economy. That is the lowest in 30 years. That is a far cry from the close to 20 per cent share that was achieved during the time the hon. member was in government.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is proud of the targets set out in his budget, but Canadian Bond Rating Service Limited explained its decision to lower the credit rating of federal government bonds by referring to the fact that since 1988 this government had been systematically off target in meeting its deficit projections.
Oral Questions
I therefore ask the Minister of Finance how he can challenge the agency's decision, considering certain facts that clearly demonstrate the incompetence and poor management of his Conservative government. How can he do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member was following market trends, it appears quite obvious that international investors have totally dismissed and disregarded the CBRS announcement because it was based on erroneous information.
Today, Moody's Investors Service issued a statement saying that it has no plans to cut Canadian debt ratings. Canada's foreign currency rating was affirmed at AAA and was reaffirmed at AAA on January 28 after a three-month review period. Standard & Poor's also says it has no plans to lower Canadian debt ratings. Of course the hon. member knows these are the most prestigious and most followed international credit advisors and credit rating agencies.
The CBRS statement can only be dismissed as being erroneous and not having much impact.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
The U.S. budget director said that NAFTA in its present form was dead in the water. However, this government is using its remaining weeks in power to try and force ratification of the NAFTA agreement as is.
My question to the Prime Minister is this: Why will the government not renegotiate an agreement that would be more in line with Canada's interests and why is it so anxious for Parliament to adopt an agreement even before it has been negotiated at the international level?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all the President of the United States and the trade commissioner of the

April 28, 1993
Oral Questions
United States have rejected the comments of Mr. Panetta. As a matter of fact I was watching with great interest last night when the President commented. I think I am quoting him correctly when he said that Mr. Panetta had a bad day when he made that statement.
The President of the United States, the President and the Government of Mexico and the Prime Minister and his government in Canada are dedicated to having the free trade agreement passed to become effective on January 1, 1994 and we are proceeding in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why the Conservative government always thinks it is better to cave in first and negotiate later which is what it is doing in this particular initiative.
I ask the minister to respond specifically to the fact that the Mack truck plant in Oakville, Ontario is being closed in a power play by the American company and the American union, even though it was the most productive of the Mack truck plants across North America.
Instead of ramming the NAFTA through Parliament why is the minister not renegotiating the deal to close the trade loophole through which the Americans right now are driving a Mack truck? What is the government afraid of?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member knows full well that any decision made by Mack truck has nothing to do with the free trade agreement. It has absolutely nothing to do with it whatsoever.
Companies rationalize and of course the Liberal Party in living back about 30 or 40 years does not understand that. There is a great deal of rationalization in the private sector. There is a great deal of rationalization in the public sector as well and we will see these types of things happen. We are also seeing rationalization taking place where companies are coming back and consolidating in Canada and closing down plants in the United States. It works both ways and the hon. member knows that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who has accomplished the impossible. He has brought in a budget that has caused outrage in virtually every part of the Canadian economy and right across Canadian society. Even his own corporate friends have said the government has brought in an inappropriate budget.
For the first time this country's credit rating is going down. The dollar is dropping. Interest rates are going up. Will the Minister of Finance now admit, with the condemnation that his budget has received across the country, that what this government is doing is wrong and not in the best interests of the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who gets up and asks the question with glee had better wipe the smile off his face because what the budget has achieved is it has driven a wedge between the federal NDP and the provincial NDP.
Imagine this, Mr. Speaker: "Federal New Democrats are sharply criticizing Ontario's Bob Rae for what they call the provincial NDP government's Draconian attempts to cut the deficit. In an unprecedented break in party unity, federal NDP finance critic Steven Langdon says Rae is on the wrong track".

Mr. Speaker, I want to say to my hon. friend what a member of the House has stated about the Rae government is not supported by this federal caucus. This federal caucus is strongly behind the Rae government in its actions in Ontario.
I noticed that the minister chose-
Oh, oh.
The hon. member for Kamloops has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I want to go back to the Minister of Finance and point out that he refused to answer my question. I will repeat it for him. The budget that was brought in did absolutely nothing to assist those
April 28, 1993

Oral Questions
four million Canadians who are either unemployed or underemployed. Those who were calling for serious deficit and debt reduction have been ignored.
Will the Minister of Finance not acknowledge the fact that his budget, after eight and a half years, reflects the mismanagement of this particular government in dealing with the economy? Should he not do the honourable thing for Canada and Canadians and offer his resignation to the Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Liberals do not agree with that. However, I am sure the Liberals are as concerned as I am about what the hon. member has just done. We have now discerned more division within the NDP ranks and he has just repudiated the party's finance critic. He has literally fired him on the floor of the House of Commons. What a shameful, shameful gesture.
Shame.
Resign.

Mr. Speaker, in the media today there was reference to the budget and this government as being a lame duck government. It is not a lame duck; it is a dead duck government and this budget reflects that.
Forget the Minister of Finance, I want to ask my friend the Prime Minister: Will he not acknowledge the fact that after eight and a half years of fiscal mismanagement, after eight and a half years of being in office, this country still has the same levels of debt and deficit and that nearly four million people are either unemployed or underemployed? Will the Prime Minister not do the right thing, send hope to the people of Canada and ask the Minister of Finance to step down from that position?

Mr. Speaker, this is indeed an historic day. There has been the repudiation of the finance critic of the NDP. There has been further division between the federal and provincial NDPs and now, in terms of what has just transpired, they are going to have to get rid of that national anthem of Solidarity Forever because it is gone.
I do not want to hurt Mr. Rae, but I think most members of the House would indicate that the premier
of Ontario is on the right track in deficit reduction. He is trying to contain the cost of government expenditures. I regret that this finds disfavour with the federal NDP because it is the same policy that Mr. Romanow is pursuing and that Mr. Harcourt is pursuing.
The leader in this has been the Minister of Finance. I point out to my hon. friends one fact only, and they can make up their minds whether they think it is valuable. In 15 years program expenditures in Ottawa increased at a rate of 13.8 per cent a year, every single year for 15 years. In the last nine years this rate of increase has been reduced to 3.8 per cent. I think that is a remarkable tribute to this Minister of Finance as well as his predecessor.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
It is obviously very embarrassing and unfortunate for a government to have the Auditor General of Canada point a finger at it. It is unfortunate and embarrassing to see a Conservative government, especially after nine years in power, trying to hide the whole truth about the increase in the budget deficit.
In an article in today's Globe and Mail, Mr. Desautels, the Auditor General of Canada said and I quote: "This is not the first time it has happened. There is very little information in the budget explaining why we are off target by so much this year".
I therefore want to ask the Minister of Finance why he can provide no clear justification for a deficit that will be $8 billion over his own 1992 projections.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very glad to provide that information to the Auditor General because it is public knowledge.
I outlined that in detail during the December statement. I indicated that the slippage in the deficit was caused totally by the slippage in revenues which I estimated at $8 billion at that time.
In the budget I explained a further deterioration that had occurred since that time to the tune of about $1.1

April 28, 1993
Oral Questions
billion. It has been the slippage and the deterioration in revenues that have caused the slippage in the deficit.
That is indeed public knowledge. I would be very glad to provide it to the hon. member and certainly send it over to the Auditor General.

Mr. Speaker, for two years the Auditor General has called upon the government to publish a score-card with the budget to compare results with projections. Obviously the Tory government does not want Canadians to see the score-card of the tired old government that has lost control of the budget reins.
The Auditor General suggests that unless the government explains in detail why it so widely missed the mark on the deficit this year, last year and the year before, Canadians should be sceptical about the projections of this year's budget.
I ask the Minister of Finance: Why should Canadians believe his projections or those projections this year when he has missed the mark in the last four years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions posed there and I hope I can answer them all.
First and foremost that is precisely why I made a statement in December, to lay before Parliament, indeed the public of Canada, the state of the financial affairs of the nation. I did it very openly. I did it again in the course of the budget. That information is all public knowledge.
The hon. member questions my figures. I am projecting a growth rate this year of something under 3 per cent. The IMF, in its latest forecast just issued yesterday, said that it sees Canada's growth rate for 1993 at 3.2 percent. Next year, 1994, it says that the growth rate for Canada will be 4.4 per cent, much in line with what we are providing.
I repeat and I say to my hon. friend who has been a long-standing member of this House and has seen Liberal years and Conservative years that he will know when we assumed office in 1984 the deficit to GDP at the time was 8.7 per cent. We have cut it in half. It will be 4.5
per cent this year and going down to .9 per cent at the end of the fiscal framework presented in this budget.

Mr. Speaker, the budget presented on Monday resulted in a decline in the value of the Canadian dollar, a rise in the bank rate, Canadian debt being downgraded by the CBRS and unprecedented criticism of the budgetary process by the Auditor General of Canada.
The minister's budget does not meet the expectations of two of his cabinet colleagues when it comes to deficit reduction. It is clear the international markets have declared a lack of confidence in the minister as a result of their reaction.
In light of the lack of confidence in the minister and his budget, and given that confidence in the Minister of Finance is of vital concern to all Canadians, does the minister not have to choose between presenting a new budget and offering his resignation to the Prime Minister? Which will he choose?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that yes, there have been some jitters in the exchange market that have been overcome. The market is strengthening. The dollar is going up and interest rates are moderating. The spreads are moderating.
I think the statement made by the Canadian Bond Rating Service has been largely dispelled by the action-
Discredited.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: -and, as my hon. friend said, discredited by the action of the major credit rating agencies, namely Standard & Poor's and Moody's. There are a number of other international financial organizations that have expressed similar scepticism about the rather curious action on the part of the Canadian Bond Rating Service agency.

I should think, Mr. Speaker, that the minister would be more concerned with the judgment of the markets which have been quite clear.
I would also like to ask him about the opening premise to his budget in which he said that there were no tax increases, yet by reducing by $625 million the amount of the GST rebate payable to low income Canadians in the
April 28, 1993

Oral Questions
current fiscal year he has effectively increased the net GST return for the current fiscal year.
Why did the minister try to pass off his budget as one that did not contain tax increases when he raised this year's GST burden on the poorest Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the hon. member's first question he was criticizing me and the government for not cutting enough. Other members have been criticizing me and the government for not cutting enough. He cannot suck and blow at the same time.
The fact of the matter is that there are $3.8 billion worth of real cuts in 1993-94. There are $5.8 billion worth of real cuts in 1994-95. There are $7.9 billion worth of real cuts in the end of the fiscal framework, for a total of $30.7 billion, the largest expenditure reduction in the history of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The news out of the U.S. is that NAFTA is dead. It is not only the opinion of Mr. Panetta but the majority of Congress. Death usually brings mourning, but the Canadian people will rejoice the death of NAFTA.
President Clinton and the U.S. Congress have indicated they will only support NAFTA if the side accords have teeth. Yesterday in committee we learned that the side accords will definitely have no teeth whatsoever. The obituary will read: NAFTA is dead.
Why is this government continuing to ram NAFTA through committee and subsequently through the House of Commons?
Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to answer that question. The larger question though is: Where has the NDP gone? They have left the House to have a special caucus on unity and-
Oh, oh.

On behalf of the Liberals, ourselves and others, may I just express the hope that this
break-up, this lovers' quarrel, can be patched up between Toronto and the federal NDP. I think we all would like to see a return of affection.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: They are looking for a marriage counsellor.
They are looking for a marriage counsellor.
Bob White is mediating.

I will not touch that one, Mr. Speaker. My hon. friend mentions it was indicated that NAFTA was dead in the United States, and he took some pleasure in that.
This of course has been repudiated by the President of the United States, by Speaker Thomas Foley who said the treaty will be approved, by Labour Secretary Robert Reich, by U.S. trade representative Mickey Kantor, by Senate majority leader George Mitchell and by the spokesman for the White House.
My hon. friend may have want of a different question. My hon. friend says: "Maybe Brian Mulroney is on his last legs". I will tell him I will be gone before NAFTA is.
Why don't you take it with you?

I am somewhat impressed, Mr. Speaker, with the Prime Minister's list but I can assure him I could provide a much longer list of congressmen opposed to NAFTA. I suspect in a vote that NAFTA will be dead.
This government strategy to ram NAFTA through is creating a legislative nightmare. Other legislation before the House will be impacted by NAFTA and will have to be changed later. Errata, which means mistakes and that is not surprising, are already being issued. Significant aspects of this bill will not be debated in the House but will be covered by regulations.
How can what amounts to an economic constitution of Canada be handled so quickly and so incompetently?

Mr. Speaker, the matter is being handled carefully and thoughtfully by the government, by members of the opposition and by others in the House. It is an important question that is in the process of being debated and considered by the House, and the House will render a

April 28, 1993
Oral Questions
judgment, a yea or nay on this. That is the way democratic institutions function.
Closure.
Closure. That is a good suggestion. Could we consider that?

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
For the last two days we have been raising questions with the minister and the Minister of National Defence about the precarious situation of our troops in Bosnia. We have been told that in fact everything is under control.
This morning we learn that French defence minister Frangois Leotard has said this about French peacekeeping troops in Bosnia, and I would like to quote: "If questions as simple as the definition of mission, the clarity of command and the sufficient finances are not resolved, we will withdraw our troops".
Clearly the French defence minister is deeply concerned about the situation of their troops. His decision puts in real jeopardy our own peacekeeping operation in Bosnia.
I want to ask the minister: Have they had discussions with the French to discuss these concerns raised by the French defence minister? How does it impact upon the security of our own troops who are presently facing renewed fighting around Srebrenica? Is the minister finally going to do something about clarifying the role of our troops in that veiy difficult theatre of operations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is quoting the French minister out of context, but let me say that all of us have concerns.
There is no country which has troops in Bosnia and indeed many which do not have troops in Bosnia which is not concerned about the situation there on the ground and the kinds of actions that we can be looking at in
terms of how to resolve this very difficult situation. I have never suggested that we have not had concerns.
What I have said is that by working closely with our military and all of the allies which are involved in the theatre in Bosnia, we feel that everything is being done that can be done and should be done to accomplish the mission. Our commanding officers in the field and our three officers in headquarters at the United Nations obviously reflect the realities back to us as to what they feel the situation is. We will continue to have those concerns.
If we did not feel that our Canadians could accomplish their missions, then we would raise it with the United Nations. When we have concerns, we do that and we will continue along the path we are taking now.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister well knows, the French have over 5,000 troops. They are the best equipped contingent within the UN arrangement in Bosnia.
If the French follow through with their threat to withdraw their troops, it puts our contingent in a very serious and very precarious situation.
It really points out the unresolved issue that we have sent troops to handle humanitarian missions. They are now being asked to protect enclaves and to protect civilians but there has been no clarity from the UN or from our government or anybody else as to exactly what the rules of engagement or the terms of that operation should be.
I want to ask the minister: Is it not time that we had a serious debate in this House of Commons about the role of our peacekeepers in Bosnia and that this government seek to ensure that if we are going to be asked to protect civilians in Bosnia that our troops are properly equipped and properly given the kind of support needed to complete that mission?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It's an opposition day tomorrow, Lloyd.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite aside from the fact that tomorrow is an opposition day, and I am sure the hon. member could raise whatever he wishes to raise in this debate, I would certainly be interested in knowing from him what he thinks we should be doing.
April 28, 1993

Does he think we should withdraw the people that we have there? Does he think that we should abandon the humanitarian effort? Does he think that we should abandon the United Nations on the ground and all the people we are assisting?
What is your position?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have made my position and the position of the government very clear in terms of our troops both in Srebrenica and in other parts of Bosnia.
As the hon. member knows, I am hoping to go there next week. I will meet with our people on the ground. In the meantime we have excellent communications with our people there. We will continue to take their advice and to work closely with our allies.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Minister of National Defence acknowledged on Monday that there is a concern over secrecy and that the public has a right to be informed about the difficult events in Somalia.
On the other hand, the minister set up a behind closed doors inquiry whose report she can censor and continues to refuse to answer very specific questions about what she knew, when she knew it and what she did about it.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. If the government is so concerned about not prejudicing the investigation which will take place, why will the Minister of National Defence not have an open public inquiry that will review the situation of our troops in Somalia and also review very carefully the role of the Minister of National Defence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister said on several occasions and indeed as the Judge Advocate General has indicated, it would be most inappropriate to go into the details of the case
Oral Questions
while the investigation is going on. The hon. member knows that. He knows that details cannot be discussed.
In terms of the inquiry, the inquiry was announced by the minister on Monday. The mandate of that organization and the people will be announced by the chief of defence staff this afternoon at 3.30 p.m. There will be civilian individuals on it. Obviously the inquiry has to be in camera because the kind of information adduced could be prejudicial to the investigations under way and make it impossible for justice to occur.
The intent of the government is to seek the truth and not to ascribe motive or lay blame. It is absolutely false of the hon. member to claim that the Minister of National Defence will censor the report before it is released.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister knows very well that there are many unanswered questions still to be discussed and answers to be provided.
For instance, why did the senior military commander in Somalia try to conceal one of the four deaths as the minister claimed? Why was the minister not told it was a homicide for two weeks, so the minister claims?
Now General MacKenzie, a retired general of the Armed Forces, said: "I am very concerned for the morale of our troops in Somalia".

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: And he said the Liberals and the NDP are causing the downfall of the morale.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The inquiry announced by the minister of defence is being held from the point of view of a person who had to find some way to deflect or to delay.
My question to the government House leader is why is the government trying to whitewash this matter? Why not have an open public inquiry and give everyone an opportunity to participate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again the hon. member has made false statements.
He indicated that the minister of defence did not know about the situation and did not take the appropriate

April 28, 1993
Oral Questions
action. That is false. The situation was brought to her attention immediately and an investigation was done as per the regime in the military.
That led to the requirement to send out an investigating team from Ottawa. That investigation is under way. Again I repeat, I wish the hon. member would have respect for our legal system and recognize that the kind of thing he is asking for would be prejudicial to the individuals involved.
In terms of former General MacKenzie's comments, what he was saying, the kinds of questions asked in this House by the Liberals and NDP have been damaging to the reputation of the Armed Forces. That is precisely what he has been saying.
What we seek through this board of inquiry is an independent board with civilians on it who can look into the situation, report back in a relatively short timeframe. In the meantime, I wish hon. members of the opposition would show respect for the men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces who are doing outstanding work in Somalia and other places around the world.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Last Friday, central Timiskaming was dealt a major blow with the provincial government cancelling 200 job relocations by the ministry of natural resources. There was the closing down of the agriculture college involving 50 jobs.
The area is now facing 35 per cent unemployment. Over the past 20 years, 127 townships have been under a land caution with no development. Both the Ontario and the Supreme Courts have ruled but the province insists that the federal government should be at the table for negotiating settlements.
Can the minister tell my constituents if the province is correct that the federal government should be at the table?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wrote last week to the minister of native affairs for the province of
Ontario and Chief Potts of the Teme-Augama Anishna-bai band arising out of the finding of the Supreme Court of Canada in 1991 that the treaty rights of the Teme-Augama Anishnabai had been adequately dealt with by way of the Robinson-Huron treaty which was signed over a century ago and that any further disputes between the province of Ontario and the Teme-Augama Anishnabai could be dealt with by the negotiation of a treaty between those two parties and that the federal government would deal with any outstanding claims against us through our specific claims policy.
Those negotiations should proceed between the two other parties.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Minister of the Environment.
Canadians are extremely worried about the disappearing ozone layer. There are record high levels of ozone depletion. It is 24 per cent over Ottawa today.
I ask the person speaking for the Minister of the Environment how much money this government has allocated to research the impacts and adaptation to ultraviolet B radiation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in the House on Friday there are a number of initiatives that this government has taken with respect to the ozone layer.
That is not only in ensuring that Canadians are aware of the changes that potentially could impact on them but on the broader research side and in the leadership position with the Montreal protocol dealing with ozone.
Our continuing efforts to work collaboratively with the provinces is not only to get rid of the existing substances which cause the depletion of the ozone layer but also to ensure that we are not adding to that.
This is an ongoing activity under our green plan with a number of departments in the provinces and we, indeed, intend to meet our targets and in fact hopefully even better them.
April 28, 1993

My supplementary is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I ask the same question I asked this time last year.
Right now tens of thousands of Canadians are developing skin cancer and cataracts because of exposure to cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation. I ask the minister again this year if he will finally introduce legislation to rate and test UV protection of both sunscreens and sunglasses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member knows that the Minister of the Environment in collaboration with the Department of National Health and Welfare made a declaration last year and strengthened the sun exposure regulations.
In terms of the legislation we are still working with the Department of the Environment and when there is reason to believe that the legislation is necessary we will pass the legislation. So far the Minister of the Environment has worked in a way that we believe it should work in terms of the necessity at the time and that which we still have.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works and it is my standard question about the fixed link.
The fixed link remains a key to transportation and development in Atlantic Canada. I see where the public works department has begun public hearings for the second time. Could the minister outline the future of the fixed link and if it is approved by the panel when can construction begin?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to my colleague on this very important private sector initiative.
Public Works Canada is presently conducting a section 12 determination pursuant to the recent Federal Court decision. Public meetings to give residents on both sides of the strait an opportunity to become familiar with this
Oral Questions
specific environmental evaluation documentation and provide their comments will be ample. These comments will be taken into consideration when the section 12 decision is made.
In addition and according to the environmental assessment review guidelines order, public works will continue to invite comments on the section 12 decision.
The premier of Prince Edward Island and I have had recent discussions and we can count on her co-operation on the constitutional issues.
I am surprised to hear my colleague from the Annapolis Valley who was part of this House and who can attest from long experience what is required to help the region and to help transportation and economic development take such a short-sighted and counter-productive view of this important project.

Mr. Speaker, in last year's budget this government projected an unemployment rate of 9.5 per cent. Now it is projecting an unemployment rate of 11.1 per cent for this year. Clearly the economy is getting worse.
The absence of an economic plan in this budget clearly reveals that this government is exhausted, lacks ideas, and the political will to bring about positive change in Canada.
My question is for the Minister of Finance. When will the minister realize that his stay the course, do-nothing approach has devastated the lives of millions of Canadians? When will this minister change the course?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again may I simply point out to the hon. member that based upon the latest IMF forecast we are projecting Canada to have the fastest growth in the G-7 countries at 3.2 per cent this year and 4.4 per cent next year.
I remind the hon. member that there were 200,000 new full-time jobs created since last August, 48,000 jobs created last month. We are expecting 300,000 new jobs created from the fourth quarter of 1992 to the fourth quarter of 1993 and over 400,000 jobs in the next year.

April 28, 1993
Routine Proceedings
We expect to bring unemployment down to 7.5 per cent by the end of the fiscal framework.

Mr. Speaker, for nine years this government has asked Canadians to sacrifice themselves to build a strong economy for future generations.
This do-nothing budget however gives no hope to the over 420,000 young people who are presently unemployed and the hundreds of thousands of students who will be looking for summer employment.
Why has this government turned its back on Canadian youth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that since we have come to office Canada has had the second best rate of growth in the G-7 and the best rate of job creation of all the G-7 countries.
The February 1992 budget, the December statement and this budget provide the basis and foundation for long-term sustained growth and price stability, job creation and a growing economy and at the same time contain the deficit.
Yesterday they were raising Cain with me because the budget was cutting too much and was not satisfying the needs of the big business community. Today they are taking a different approach and I can only concur with the findings-
We must push on. The hon. member for Willowdale.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to the finance minister's prognostications, we know how wrong his forecasting has been in the past.
The legacy of this government as it leaves office is a $30 billion high-tech trade deficit, a fall from fourth to eleventh place in our ability to compete, 16 per cent of our manufacturing jobs lost in the last four years and 11 per cent unemployment, the highest in the G-7. This is the Tory economic legacy.
Why did the government not use last Monday's budget, its last chance, to introduce a comprehensive economic strategy, a means to get rid of the
deindustrialization of Canada and get Canadians back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I disagree fundamentally with the hon. member. He knows that we have had the second best productivity rate in the G-7. That is showing up in our ability to compete and our ability to achieve exports and that does create jobs. Our exports to the United States have increased by over 21 per cent which is the highest in history.
Here is the legacy: Let us look at Canada's industrial production over the last three months compared to other countries and I know the hon. member will really take this into consideration. This shows the trend. Canada's industrial production is growing at the rate of 4.3 per cent, the U.S. at 4.1 per cent, Japan at minus 5.3 per cent, Germany at minus 11.2 per cent, France at minus
3.7	per cent, U.K. at 1.7 per cent, and Italy at minus 2.9 per cent. I can say that I am proud of that legacy.

Madam Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to ensure that there is a standard school leaving age across Canada and the federal money that is contributed to the provinces for post-secondary education is used solely for that purpose.
The reason for this is because a lot of the money that the federal government gives to the provinces for education is not being used by the provinces for education but for something else.
As well, the standard school leaving age across Canada varies from one province to the next. Therefore this bill will have a uniform standard school leaving age. It will also ensure that money given to the provinces for education is used for education.

Madam Speaker, this bill would permit registration of the pension plan allowing nurses early retirement on the same basis as is currently permitted for public safety employees. Early retirement would be available as early as age 55, for 25 years' service, a combination of age and service totalling 75 or total and permanent disability.
Currently the early retirement rights of public safety employees are governed by the income tax regulations and cover fire-fighters, police officers, corrections officers, air traffic controllers and commercial airline pilots.
This bill places the right to early retirement in the Income Tax Act and adds nurses. The amendment would be effective for 1993. It seems to me that the demands being made on nurses in today's society warrant such consideration. Income security is important, not only to them but to all Canadians and we have the responsibility to provide it.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by several residents of the province of Alberta, most of whom reside in Edmonton.
They argue that the current Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement sharply reduces the power of all Canadian governments to develop the Canadian economy. They argue that more than 400,000 Canadian manufacturing jobs have been lost since the FTA became law in 1989 and that if implemented the North American free trade agreement will cause even more Canadian jobs to be lost.
They call on the House to reject the proposed North American free trade agreement and recommend to the government that it use the FTA's termination clause to end the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.

subsubtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present a petition on behalf of many Canadians who call on Parliament to amend the Canada Labour Code to prohibit the use of replacement workers by employers during a strike or lockout in federal jurisdictions.

subsubtopic: SERIAL KILLER BOARD GAME
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 36 to present a petition from 27 very conscientious and serious citizens of my hometown of Wolfville, Nova Scotia in regard to outlawing the serial killer board game which I know has come up in this House before.
Quite frankly I think it is appropriate because of the repugnance of this game to read the first whereas of this petition. The petition reads: Whereas the parents and grandparents seek a ban of a new game to be introduced in Canada called the serial killer board game; whereas this game comes with a body bag, 25 babies and four serial killer figures, the object of which is to commit murder and the person with the highest body count being
Routine Proceedings
the winner. The petitioners further state that this game is not in the best interest of children and in the wrong hands could become dangerous and they suggest it could easily impress young people.
Therefore my petitioners humbly pray, as I think all members in this House agree, that this type of obscenity should not be allowed in Canada. I hope the government continues to proceed to ban it.

subsubtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the privilege of presenting to Parliament the signatures of hundreds of Greek Canadian citizens from my riding.
The petition states that the Government of Canada has decided to amend the Canadian war veterans act so that effective March 2, 1992 persons are no longer eligible for benefits under the war veterans allowance program based on resistance service only.
Therefore the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to accept legislation designed to rescind the above mentioned amendment in order to stop the discrimination between Canadian veterans of the resistance movements and veterans of the formal military capacity since all were fighters against the enemy of Canada, stop the discrimination between Canadian citizens who should all have equal rights in terms of where they live and receive their rightful benefits and deal in a humane manner with senior citizens who after many years of work and service to Canada are now forced to again move back under often veiy difficult conditions.
