speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the House rose yesterday, there were two minutes left for the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. After that we will proceed with questions and comments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will continue where I left off yesterday and will conclude by saying that the Canadian economy is moving along well.
It is probably not moving as fast as we would like but as I indicated yesterday, most economic think tanks and the International Monetary Fund have predicted that Canada's economy will outpace those of all other industrialized countries in the next couple of years.
There are a number of reasons for that and not just the major ones that were introduced two days ago by the Minister of Finance. It simply builds upon the consistent
April 28, 1993

sound fundamental management of the economy by the government since 1984.
It also builds upon our economic statement last December in this House. As evidence of that we have had a tremendous turnaround in the economy. In fact as the minister noted in the House today, 200,000 jobs have been created in Canada since August of last year and
48,000	new jobs were created last month alone.
In addition to that, we can go back to the heart of many of these budgets introduced. In fact 148,000 Canadians took advantage of the housing program announced a year ago regarding the use of RRSP contributions toward the construction of a new home. That is one indication of what we have done on this side of the House in recent months. There is the reduction in personal income tax and changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Those things are all adding to the base that we set in 1984. I am quite proud of that record. I will entertain questions and comments from the other side of the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again I find myself having a difference with the member for Carleton-Charlotte. This has been a repeated exercise over many months. I must tell him that I have a lot of respect for the member when he talks about this approach to the fundamentals being in place. I understand where he is coming from. I recognize the lower interest rates and I recognize practically no inflation in this country. However, in our communities now because of this obsession with zero inflation we have between the welfare rolls and the unemployment rolls well over three million people out of work.
We agreed on both sides of the House in the last four months that the key to creating new jobs really did lie with the small business sector. All parties put the Small Businesses Loans Act through the House. I am sure that Canadians have heard more about the Small Businesses Loans Act in the last 90 days than they had in the previous 15 years.
The problem I have with the government on the Small Businesses Loans Act is that it is not honouring the commitment it made in this House just two months ago. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism
The Budget
stood up in this House and said that he was going to have a promotional package so that the small business community would be aware that this particular instrument was out there for small businesses to use. That has not happened.
I know that Scotiabank has taken out some ads in the paper and I commend Scotiabank for that. I commend the Bank of Montreal for coming in at one point under prime for loans under $100,000.
Does the member not really believe that this recovery cannot happen unless the banks are aggressively promoting and utilizing the Small Businesses Loans Act? If the member does believe that is necessary then what will he and his government do to make sure that happens?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no question that small business is the backbone of the Canadian economy. That is where most jobs occur. The biggest single employer is the small business sector.
We have done many things on this side of the House as a government and with the support of some members opposite in that regard. Of course, the changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act to which the member refers is an example of that.
I did in fact put that question to the minister responsible for small businesses, as the member acknowledges, not too long ago in this House because that has always been a concern of mine. We do what is necessary in this House but we expect co-operation from those lending institutions outside of this House to really make it happen on the street. I acknowledge that that has not happened in previous years up until these changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act.
There are provisions within the Small Businesses Loans Act that make it more lucrative for the banks to become involved with small business. There is an indication that is happening but rest assured-and I will say this to the member from Broadview-Greenwood as well-I will continue to press the minister to make sure it does happen.
I know the Minister of Finance was a small business owner at one time and is very sensitive in this regard. I am going to continue to hold the banks' feet to the fire and make sure it does respond to legislation brought into this House because it is very important.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
There are many small businesses out there that are cash starved. They are not asking government to do anything for them. They are simply asking the banks to respond in a positive way and I hope they will. Rest assured I am going to do my best to make sure they do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to ask my colleague two questions.
He indicated there has been some management on the part of the government and the basics are in place. How can he say that, and I do not say it unkindly, when right now well over 1.6 million Canadians are without work and 2.7 million Canadians are receiving social assistance? Over two million Canadians will be fed at food banks, the deficit is well in excess of $30 billion and the debt has surpassed $450 billion when it was less than $200 billion when this government came into power.
My province of Manitoba has taken five major hits. Regional development has been cut and there have been cuts to VIA Rail and CBC again and again. Mining and forestry agreements are no longer going to be in operation. There will be jobs lost in all of these areas.
How can people have hope? How can people from Manitoba and other regions think that this particular budget will help sustain what we have now and make it grow? I just do not see it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope I have time
for my response.
There is no question, as I mentioned yesterday in my speech, that 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed. None of us can take any satisfaction from that no matter which side of the House we sit on.
The point is that the Canadian economy is moving in the right direction. As evidence of that let us take a look at some of the numbers. I quoted the numbers in regard to the IMF and the predicted growth within the Canadian economy, sustained growth over the last number of years and the projections they are putting forward for next year and the year after. That is all encouraging but I go back to some of the numbers on which we can hang our hats.
For example our exports last year were at an all-time record high of $157 billion. What does that do? It translates into jobs. As I articulated earlier, 200,000 jobs
have been created since last August and 48,000 jobs were created last month alone. That is an improvement. The difficulty is that when the economy is moving along the impact of the growth will not be felt this afternoon or next week. It takes time.
Obviously the fundamentals have to be put in place so that movement continues and we have done that. I think we have to emphasize that because all of us would like to pick up the magic wand, wave it and cause unemployment to cease but that is not the way it is.
I go back to the heart of the matter. The fundamentals are in place and I think that is what the member has to take a very hard look at.
With regard to the situation in Manitoba and all the provinces, the transfers to the provinces, particularly the poorer provinces and we include Manitoba in that, have not been touched. For example the transfers to the province of Manitoba and my own home province of New Brunswick have not been touched and they will actually increase beyond increases in other sectors.
In fact the finance minister in the province of New Brunswick was very positive in his response to the budget introduced two days ago.
He said: "Listen, how can I criticize the federal government because we do have a cash crunch in this country. We do have some problems but the transfers to our province of New Brunswick are increasing as they will to Manitoba". We recognize that those provinces depend on those transfer dollars.
We are being criticized in some quarters for not having cut back on those transfer dollars but coming from one of the poorer provinces, I would say the government did the right thing in that regard.
For example, the province of New Brunswick depends on direct cash transfers from the Government of Canada for 40 per cent of its revenues. Those have been left intact and this year will amount to approximately $1.5 billion. The government can take some encouragement from that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words about this non-event that is called the budget.
April 28, 1993

I have seen a number of budgets in my day in the House of Commons and I cannot recall a budget that has been such a non-event, non-existent one composed of smoke and mirrors as the budget we have before us today.
There is scarcely a budget in this country either federally or provincially that does not have a tax change, that does not have a program change, that does not have some new initiative. Yet we have a budget here that accomplishes basically very little.
It is really a continuation of the same statement we had last year in the December economic statement. Of course, as a result of the budget, nobody is happy.
I am not happy because it does not tackle the big problem of job creation in this country. It also makes things more difficult for the farmers in the prairies, particularly in Saskatchewan. Even the friends of the government are not happy. The business community and the investment community are not happy with the government.
A bond rating company in Montreal lowered the credit rating of the Government of Canada yesterday from an AAA rating to an AA rating. I think that may be the lowest credit rating the federal government has had in history. An AA rating is very low for the federal government of this country.
The Canadian dollar went down as a result of that. The minister across the way knows that the Canadian dollar value went down. Yesterday the Bank of Canada boosted the central bank rate significantly to try to prop up the Canadian dollar. We have already had short-term immediate consequences of this budget presented by the government across the way.
There is no vision in the budget. There is no plan. There is no direction as to where this government wants to go. Despite nine years in office, 11 per cent of the Canadian people are unemployed. Another huge percentage is on welfare, working part-time, has dropped out or is underemployed.
The Canadian Council of Bishops said two weeks ago that over three million Canadians are either unemployed or underemployed in this country. What a shame for the wealthiest country in the industrialized world to have such human waste and human devastation.
The Budget
We have had nine long lean years of the Conservative Party and yet 11 per cent of our people are unemployed and over one million people are on welfare.
Let me talk about the deficit. That is like putting the skunk in the hen house. The Conservative Party talks about the deficit but what has happened to the deficit in this country? This year it is still going to be over $32 billion. Last year it was about $35 billion. In 1984 when this Prime Minister came to office the debt was about $160 billion. This year it is going to be $458 billion.
It has gone from $160 billion to $458 billion and that comes from a Conservative Party that says: "Look, keep electing us and we will control the debt and the deficit in this country". Now the leadership candidates, in particular the Minister of the Environment and the former Minister of Justice, are going around this country saying: "Look, we have some ideas on how to control the deficit and eliminate it in three years".
That is like the chicken voting for Colonel Sanders. If they have these ideas about how to get rid of the debt and the deficit, why did they not say something when they were sitting in the cabinet for the last five years to eight years? They are misleading the people of this country as the Conservative Party has historically done. The Conservative Party has destroyed this country economically. It has driven people on to the unemployment rolls by driving up the interest rates. It brought in a GST which slowed down the Canadian economy, strangled small business and made more paper work and more bureaucracy for the small business community. It brought in a trade deal with the United States that has given away our sovereignty and that is now resulting in hundreds of thousands of people losing their jobs in Ontario in particular. This loss is not temporary like in the last recession but it is permanent this time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Two-thirds of them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those jobs are moving south of the border to the United States and more recently they are starting to move south of that border into Mexico.
As my friend who is the member for Trinity-Spadina in Toronto says, about two-thirds of those lost jobs are lost permanently in the province of Ontario. It is because the government has given away too much. It has given

April 28, 1993
The Budget
away the store and destroyed this country. It has destroyed this country economically and is destroying many of the other institutions that we have in this country as well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It calls it economic management.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It gave cutbacks to CBC, VIA Rail, and the post office system. There is the destruction of rural post offices. In fact even in my small city of Yorkton with about 18,000 people, by no means a small town or a village, we lost our post office two years ago because of this government.
The government is destroying the very institutions of this country that bind us together east and west with the trade deal with the United States. Now of course we have NAFTA, which is the North American free trade agreement with Mexico and the United States.
Even the President of the United States is not happy with NAFTA. He wants to negotiate side agreements and parallel agreements. Yet we have a government now that is trying to force NAFTA through the House of Commons, dissolve this country even more in terms of north and south and to play the tune once again of large multinational corporations.
That is not good enough. Regardless of who wins the Conservative Party leadership in about six weeks, the Canadian people will know that a Conservative is a Conservative is a Conservative and this is the kind of economic policy that has been set by this government for the last nine years.
In this budget, even though it did not change very much, there were a few changes that are going to hurt ordinary people. The GST for example now has a tax credit that is paid out to the poorest Canadians four times a year. I know people in my riding who get that cheque every three months. So what is this government going to do? Instead of paying it out every four months, it is now going to pay it out every six months to the poor people. This will make it more difficult for the poor to provide for the needs of their children: food, shelter, clothing and their own lives. By doing that the government is going to save $7.5 million.
If the Prime Minister would cancel his fancy farewell tour to Europe we would probably save about $1 million. That would be more significant than stopping the payment of those cheques every three months to the poor
people so that they have some money on a regular basis to feed their families.
It is $7.5 million a year. That is important but in the over-all budget it is a very small drop in the puddle. It is a very small drop and it helps ordinary people when they need it the most. These ordinary people are going to spend that money right away. They are going to pay some of it back in taxes. They are going to stimulate the economy by buying goods and services.
Second, another change in the budget, perhaps most significant of all, is the change to the Crow benefit for prairie farmers. I think that is probably one of the only, if not the only, announcement of a legislative initiative in the budget. Look at page 53. The government says that it is going to cut back the Crow benefit by another 10 per cent. The Crow benefit was an agreement signed by the federal government to last in perpetuity to provide $720 million a year for the farmers to pay the railways to subsidize the movement of grain.
A year ago the federal government decided to cut it back by 10 per cent, some $72 million, unilaterally. That is not co-operative federalism. That is not going out and saying to the provinces and the farmers of this country: "We want your input and involvement before we make an important decision". That is the Minister of Finance reaching into farmers' pockets in my riding and in ridings across the prairies and taking out $72 million.
Now the government is saying that in the next fiscal year it is going to increase it. It is not just a 10 per cent cutback but a 15 per cent cutback. The year after that there will be a 20 per cent cutback and that will go on in perpetuity. A 20 per cent cutback is over $140 million a year. This is unless the federal government negotiates an agreement with the provinces and the farmers to change the method of payment from the railways to the farmers. If the money goes directly to the farmers then there goes the grain subsidy. There goes some orderly transportation in this country.
The wheat pools in the prairies have said to keep the money going to the railways. The National Farmers' Union has said the same thing. The Saskatchewan government has said the same thing. The people of my province have said the same thing. Yet the government across the way wants to change the method of payment to satisfy some of their wealthy friends, particularly the
April 28, 1993

large grain growers of southern Alberta and the cattle producers of the prairies.
That is nothing short of blackmail by the federal government and nothing short of a bribe. It is saying to the prairie farmers that if they do not agree to the change in the method of payment then another 10 per cent will be cut off the Crow benefit and they will lose another $72 million a year.
That is not good enough at all. We want to build a strong country and create jobs for our farmers and our people right across the country.
There is a third part that I want to mention about the budget in terms of some of the changes that are not really seen as that significant overall but in terms of people who are affected directly this is extremely important in addition to the GST and the Crow benefit. It is the announcement of further cutbacks in regional development.
My guess by looking at page 53 of the budget is that the cutback in regional development is going to amount to approximately $500 million a year. Maybe we should cut back on some things. We have a deficit problem. Why not cut back on military helicopters and save $5.8 billion rather than cut regional development in New Brunswick and Saskatchewan and northern Quebec and save-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is over 14 years. What are you talking about?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not say for a year for military helicopters. Please listen.
Why not cut back by $5.8 billion on military helicopters instead of cutting back by $500 million per year on regional development? If one comes from Atlantic Canada, northern Quebec, northern Ontario, parts of the prairies or B.C. one realizes how important it is to have money going into regional development.
The unemployment rate in Newfoundland and New Brunswick is criminally high. Yet the government is now saying we should take $500 million a year out of regional development so it can spend that money on military helicopters that we do not need.
The Budget
It is a question of priorities. Sure we have a fiscal problem and a deficit. We have a debt that is the highest of the G-7 nations. It is a matter of priorities. Take the money away from military helicopters. Bring in a fair tax system so the rich pay their fair share and so corporations pay their fair share. Plug some of the loopholes in the tax system. Get rid of capital gains exemption of $100,000 except for farmers and people with their principal homes. It will then raise more money and there will be more revenue for people to spend. If we have more revenue we will tackle the debt problem. If we have more revenue we will save our social programs.
Finally the most important thing of all is a jobs plan. We are one of the few countries in the world that does not have a jobs plan. If one looks at Europe, Japan and the new administration in the United States they are talking about how to put people back to work and how to create more wealth and how to actually get people producing something and paying taxes for the benefit of the country and society.
The only way to reduce the debt in a real and meaningful way is to create jobs so that people are off welfare and unemployment insurance and are contributing taxes to the government of Canada and taxes to the provinces.
If we put another half a million people to work the debt will go down. We will have more cash for the social programs and the other programs that are so desperately needed.
Our party said about two months ago that we had a plan and strategy for full employment. It was announced by our leader. It is a plan that would see our country investing more money in research and development. We are among the worst in the industrialized world in terms of the mere pittance we put into research and development today. We are also among the worst in terms of the money we spend in training our workers for the new challenges that lie ahead.
There are a lot of areas in this country where we could be investing money in terms of infrastructure. There are a number of things we could also be doing well, things that are natural for our country to do well if we spent more money on them.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
We could be investing in things like transportation, communications, agriculture, mining, forestry, resources of that sort and investing more in the environment, an issue that is becoming more and more important every day. We could put more money into social housing, co-op housing and things of that sort. These are things that should be done but are not done by the government across the way.
If we are to solve the debt problem, if we are to get rid of some of the human misery we see today, we are going to have to put every single ounce of our energy into a national job strategy that involves not just the federal government but the provinces and the territories, the trade unions, the farm sector and the private business sector as well.
There should be an assault on unemployment and poverty like the assault we had during the Second World War. If we were able to mobilize our resources for combat in the First World War, the Second World War or other wars throughout history, surely to goodness we can mobilize this country's resources to fight unemployment and put people back to work. This would give them some dignity and pride in their own lives and help them make a contribution to their own economy.
I do not have too many more minutes left but before I finish I would like to say that Saskatchewan is a prime example of what Conservatives have done to this country in the last eight or nine years. We are a province that is now losing people. We now have the highest unemployment we have ever had in the history of our province. It is up about 8 per cent or 9 per cent. We are a province in which more and more people are on welfare. More and more people are dropping out. They are disillusioned. We are a province now that is losing farmer after farmer each and every single day. We are losing our small towns and villages.
Despite that the federal government in the last few years has been cutting back every year, except this year, on transfers to the provinces in terms of health, education and equalization. It has cut back on the increase. It has cut back in my province by some $500 million over what it would have been if the formulas had not changed. These are the changes in the formula for equalization and the changes in the formula for transfers under the fiscal arrangements we have in this country.
We now have a province that is worse off than it was in the 1930s. For nine years we also had a Conservative government with Grant Devine as premier. The province when he took over in 1982 had a debt of some $3.5 billion. Nine years later, our debt is now about $15 billion, the highest per capita debt anywhere in this country, including Newfoundland and Labrador. Nine long, lean years of Conservative government and the debt goes from $3.5 billion to some $14 billion in the province of Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's just not true. Thlk about the operating surplus.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I invite the noisy member from the Conservative Party across the way to come to Saskatchewan and make some of those comments. He would be driven out of town.
We are now in a position where because of Conservative governments hospitals are being closed down, rural communities are being destroyed, the province is on the brink of bankruptcy. That is the Conservative legacy. A Conservative legacy is one where there is no vision, where there is no dream about what this country could be.
We need a change in this country. We need a change badly. We need a government that will put jobs first, a government that will put people first. We need a government that will rescind the trade deal to regain some of our sovereignty we have lost because of the free trade agreement with the United States. We need a government that will get rid of the GST and bring in a fair tax system based on the ability to pay.
These are things the Conservative Party has done to destroy this country. Another four years of the Conservative Party and I fear for the future of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is quite amusing to listen to a member of the New Democratic Party speak of the difficulties in Saskatchewan.
Those members forget that their own party formed the Government of Saskatchewan. Who do you blame? When he is laying blame and pointing fingers in Saskatchewan I think he has to point fingers at his own party and his own premier. But let me take him up on some of the other points in his speech.
April 28, 1993

One of the things he mentioned was that this country would be a lot better off in terms of debt if we had half a million more people working. Well, if he would just watch the Canadian economy grow and if he looked at the statistics which are there for everyone to see, he would be quite pleased. Since August we have created
200.000	full-time jobs and last month alone there were
48.000	new jobs in Canada. So with that kind of a track record he will not have to wait too long to see an extra
500.000	people employed in Canada.
Sorting through what he has said and one must examine it very carefully, for example, the free trade agreement with the United States of America. In the last year alone for our trade component we have had $157 billion in exports, 80 per cent of which were exported to the United States. That is the largest total in the history of Canada. It is working very much in our favour.
If we want to see the Canadian economy grow, let us continue with what we are doing. Let us not throw out some of the policies that are working. We can always come under scrutiny on anything we do as a government, but examine the facts and examine them very carefully. Do not forget who is the premier of Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased that my friend across the way said not to forget who is the premier of Saskatchewan. The premier is Roy Romanow. He took over from Grant Devine, who in nine years drove the debt in our province up from $3.5 billion to $15 billion. That is without precedent anywhere in this country, including during the 1930s and the Great Depression. Nowhere in this country on a per capita basis, perhaps nowhere in North America, has a debt gone up as quickly as it did in Saskatchewan during the Conservative years of Grant Devine.
After 17 months of government Premier Roy Romanow has cut our deficit in half and he has done that without the help of the federal government. He has done that despite the fact that the rate of increase in transfers to the province has gone down, which has cost us over $500 million in the last year. He has done that despite the fact that the federal government across the way has promised time and time again a third line of defence to help prairie farmers, but yet has reneged on that prom-
The Budget
ise, so that money is not there and many farmers are living in poverty.
No, I have not forgotten who is the premier of Saskatchewan. The premier of Saskatchewan is cleaning up the mess the Conservative Party left our province in over the last nine years, as had to be done a number of years ago after the 1930s. I say to my friend across the way that when the debt goes from $3.5 billion to $15 billion in nine years something is seriously wrong.
The people in my province will not vote Conservative again for at least another generation because of the legacy Grant Devine has left behind. There is no party in this House that has less credibility in the debt issue in Canada than the Conservative Party sitting across the way.
In the 1930s it was Prime Minister Bennett, a Conservative prime minister, who brought us the Great Depression and brought us debts right across this country. In the 1980s it was Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and Premier Grant Devine who did the same thing in this country and in my province. The people of my province will not forget.

The Budget

I am glad the member raised this point. There will certainly be difficulties in the province of Ontario when a lot of things have to be done that are not very easy and not very comfortable. At least in Ontario he is consulting the trade unions and the public sector trade unions in the province.
In Manitoba with Conservative Premier Gary Filmon there was no consultation whatsoever with the public sector when he decided to dock the public servants several days of work. They did not consult the public sector unions. They did not negotiate with them. They did not do anything at all with them in terms of a consultative process. All of a sudden they just announced it: "You take days off without pay".
That is not the way to run a country. At least in Ontario Bob Rae is sitting down with members of the public sector, negotiating with them and talking with them about the very serious problem facing the province of Ontario. He is doing the right thing. In principle I believe he is doing the right thing. I cannot comment on all the details in Ontario as I am not familiar with them.
I know in my own province of Saskatchewan that the premier has done a commendable job in a very difficult situation. The people of our province are behind the premier in terms of trying to get control of the economy once again. If we do not get control of our own economy, it is going to be run by the bankers and the international investment traders and we are going to have even less flexibility in terms of protecting our social programs and doing what we should be doing as Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are times when circumstances dictate a change in course for the ship of state. That is what we had to do in 1984. At that time, as everyone will remember, we were headed straight for the rocks.
April 28, 1993

The Budget
At other times the course is maintained because only some minor adjustments are needed to continue to make progress. No one should be surprised that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, did exactly that in the budget which he tabled on Monday and which I support without reservation.
In the past eight years, our government did the right thing at the right time for our economic strength. We should not be surprised that not everyone was pleased with this. Some think that the budget should have provided more drastic spending reductions. Others think that their favourite program should have received more funding from the government or that we should have adopted the solution that they advocate.
The money market had certain expectations and some credit rating agencies had others.

Some wanted short-term solutions to immediate problems and others wanted nothing that was not directed to long-term gains. In each case it was the task of the Minister of Finance to find the balance and do the right thing for Canadians, and that is exactly what he did.
All the comments we have heard about last wills and testaments and the labelling of existing programs as instant job creation projects is the height of irresponsibility. It is easy to become a 10-second hero by delivering clever second guesses with the principal objective of getting attention from the camera and headline writers. Perhaps some people are impressed with those who complain of government spending in one breath and who present a long wish list for spending increases in the next.
It is like St. Augustine's famous prayer: "Lord give me chastity but not just yet". Those would-be finance ministers from whom we have heard need to understand that countries are strengthened by serious reflection and wisdom, not by loose tongues craving quick attention.
Fortunately the Minister of Finance has met the expectations of most Canadians by placing before the House a budget that is realistic, responsible, coherent, achievable and right on course.

I believe that Canadians got what they learned to expect from this government: effective policies and long-term strategies that attack problems at their roots in order to find lasting solutions.
All Canadians agree that governments at all levels must get their finances in order. Canadians therefore recognize that the Minister of Finance has presented them with a budget that will maintain the same direction for five more years, so that Canada will be quite ready for the next millennium, the 21st century.
In his December economic statement the Minister of Finance emphasized the importance this government attaches to reducing the deficit so that we can attain our objective, which is to lay the foundation for lasting economic growth. Canadians want an end to the deficit and the debt which are irresponsibly mortgaging our grandchildren's right to decide their own future for themselves. They want the deficit to be reduced the right way, by reducing spending not raising taxes. That is what the Minister of Finance did. They want public spending to be restricted, but not so much that the government can no longer do its job. That is why this government has increased the efficiency of the Civil Service since 1984.
In real terms-and very few Canadians, even in this House, seem to realize it-the cost of administering the federal government is less today than it was eight years ago, although our population has grown by 10 per cent.
It is thanks to this kind of management that we can cut more than $30 billion over the next five years in this budget and overspending will not endanger the country's future prosperity. Of course the budget must be seen in the light of the many other long-term initiatives taken by the government because they are all part of a complete mutually supporting package of measures to put Canada's economy in order.
The people opposite seem to tamper with the truth about the economy. I will remind them that our ability to maintain social programs, establish environmental enterprises, be responsible members of the international community and maintain prosperity depends on a solid economic base. If this base is neglected, as they always tend to do in their simplistic, one-dimensional, magical

April 28, 1993
The Budget
proposals then none of these important objectives will be achieved.
Remember that since 1988 every budget cutting measure that we presented in this House was opposed by the opposition members of all parties. How can they get up with a straight face today and criticize the government which is trying to get public spending under control by presenting a proposal that will nearly eliminate the deficit in five years?

I resent some of the comments we hear. They talk about the unemployed. I feel deep compassion in my heart for people who are jobless. There is a recipe to help those people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was trying to say that as a government we did not choose to accept the suggestions of the opposition to inject additional new funds or to worsen the deficit. We definitely did not choose that route proposed by the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party.
They may have succumbed to the temptation in past election years but we took the responsible course of action. It is my firm belief and that of my colleagues in this party, along with many Canadians, that creating jobs is the task of the private sector. No amount of government spending of tax dollars will equal the drive and productivity of small business in creating jobs.
We did what governments should do. We have created an environment conducive to job creation by reducing the deficit. This means less borrowing, lower interest rates and lower taxes. These are all conditions that stimulate economic activity leading to more important, satisfying jobs.
In my own area of responsibility we have taken the initiative to use unemployment insurance to provide new opportunities for workers. Understanding that we find ourselves facing relentless and strong competition in the changing, knowledge-based global economy we have moved to increase work force skills so that in the years ahead Canadians can enjoy long-term rewarding employment which contributes to the prosperity of Canada.
These are times in which we simultaneously see unemployment of workers in older sectors while employers in the new sectors complain they cannot find enough workers with the necessary skills. That is the reality out there. We hear that every day.
We have shifted funds from their traditional passive use as temporary income support to active measures which will make future income support less necessary. Based on recommendations of the Canadian Labour Force Development Board we have invested $2.21 billion to help over half a million unemployment insurance recipients to renovate their job skills for the labour market of tomorrow.
That is a 19 per cent increase over the 1992 expenditure and a 400 per cent increase over the 1990 expenditure. We have increased to $110 million funds for the
April 28, 1993

self-employment assistance option which helps qualified workers to become entrepreneurs running their own businesses.
For those UI recipients who wish to arrange for their own training support will be increased to $455 million this year.

As Minister of Employment and Immigration, as I was just saying, I know how tragic unemployment is. I am aware of the suffering the unemployed go through. Imagine a man, woman or a young person anywhere in the country who wants to work and is looking for a job and is qualified to hold a job but unfortunately, due to weak market conditions, is unable to get work. The measure announced in December pays special attention to these experienced workers who for years contributed to Canada's prosperity but suddenly lost their jobs as a result of technological change.
Some skilled people held the same job for 15 or 20 years but suddenly lost it because of technological change and then they do not have the skills needed for other work. We have allocated $300 million to help these people acquire the skills that will again enable them to be productive workers. In all, we have directed $3.8 billion to labour market programs that will affect more than a million workers. Canadians will appreciate that we are working on this with other interested parties. Federal government funding has acted as a catalyst to provide the appropriate infrastructure for employers, labour, community groups and provincial governments to implement economic initiatives commensurate with their own requirements.
Pooling all sectoral resources is the only way to proceed if we want to create a society in which all Canadians will have a chance to succeed, at any stage in their lives.
I have said repeatedly that we are investing in mechanisms to help workers quickly get back on their feet and develop their full potential. We do not want to provide lifetime safety nets that keep people in a state of dependency and make them lose all initiative. That was the result of the policies developed in the 1960s and 1970s.
The Budget
We want to use our social programs to help people who have found effective solutions, who make the right choices and who are promising. I have to analyse this budget from the perspective of my department, but also from the perspective of the Atlantic region which I represent in Parliament.
In fact I can assure the House the Atlantic region has not been overlooked in this budget because in the past we in the Atlantic region have been through some difficult times, and we have always come out on top.
People in the Atlantic region have always been willing to shoulder their fair share of the burden and to adapt their expectations and institutions to meet new challenges. We knew that in the end we would be better prepared to meet the challenges of the future.
This year the federal government will spend $5.2 billion in the Atlantic region, or $2,250 per capita. I submit that the decision to exempt these transfer payments from spending cuts reflects the federal government's understanding of the fiscal problems in the Atlantic provinces due to the recession and economic restructuring.
Transfer payments to the provinces will continue to increase at a rate of 4 per cent annually, although all other government spending will be capped at 1.5 per cent, which is below the rate of inflation.

While this budget's proposals on the deficit are alone enough to earn its commendation it goes much further. It goes much further in advancing the government's long-term agenda. The finance minister has set a goal of zero cash requirements by 1997-98, at which time net new federal borrowing will be eliminated completely.
That is the way it was in Canada during our lifetimes before we got blown away by thinking that there is no day of reckoning. Once we have put ourselves back on course the government can then begin to pay down the debt which continues to sap our reserves.
Inflation has been beaten back. Interest rates are at a 20-year low. Exports are surging, as my colleague from Carleton-Charlotte pointed out earlier. Business has become increasingly competitive in Canada. Small businesses are doing much better. In both new and old marketplaces trade agreements are opening up more markets for quality Canadian goods and services.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
For the first time in decades Canadians can now clearly see the solid foundation which we have been building and on which we all can successfully compete in a very different world than the one which existed before this restructuring started.
In this and other ways this government has not shirked from any opportunity to make positive adjustments to help Canada confront these new global realities.
We know some people in this country want to wish away the challenges but that is not what we have done. The issues that everyone else has been afraid to touch were put at the top of the public agenda by this government rather than hiding them away as others have done for fear of controversy.
We did not shy away from attacking the underlying causes of problems, even at the price of popularity as measured by fickle will-o'-the-wisp polls. We had faith that over the long run Canadian men and women would see that we have done the right thing. The budget the finance minister has tabled before this House is in that category of principled action.

I agree, there is not much to rejoice about in the budget. There may be nothing to rejoice about, but there is no reason for despair either. It is a firm budget. It is a realistic budget that indicate we have a long way to go. It makes no unreasonable demands but continues to deal gradually with the consequences of past excesses. It reflects the fact that Canadians understand there is no easy, quick solution to our problems, although there are still politicians proposing the so-called quick fix. This budget states the facts clearly and honestly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not believe for one second that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is happy presiding over this nation's current condition of unemployment. Under his reign we have the highest rate of unemployment in the history of Canada. We have over three million people now looking for work in this country.
Whether it is 3.1 million or 3.2 million the bottom line is that we have a crisis of unemployment in this country. I believe the hon. minister wants to fix this problem as much as any other member in this House. He must want to fix it.
However I believe there is a very important point that the government is missing. As Liberals we stood up in this House of Commons over the last three months and supported the government's initiative called the Small Businesses Loans Act. We supported it, we did not criticize it. We worked together and came up with amendments. Last year I think it cost the Treasury $29 million from the float in write-offs to small businesses but if we take into account the benefits in employment measures it cannot be criticized. It is a good piece of legislation.
The problem is that the financial institutions of Canada, the banks, the credit unions and others that could be eligible to lend money under the Small Businesses Loans Act are not making that act work. So when we come to the floor of this House of Commons and try to bring attention to this problem but do not seem to get any reaction we get terribly frustrated.
My question to the minister is a very simple one: Is he satisfied with the way the financial institutions of this country, the banks and the credit unions, are treating small business? Is that why we hear nothing from the government in terms of chastising, pushing or motivating banks? Is he satisfied? If he is satisfied that is fine. It is a simple yes and I will sit down.
However if he is not satisfied, could he commit on behalf of his government, the small business community and the unemployed that he will take a message to the cabinet of Canada, the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of Finance and say: let us do something to move the financial institutions of this country to honour an act of Parliament that was passed by all parties in this House?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know if this has ever occurred to the member concerning these financial institutions and banks but it is Canadians' savings that these financial institutions and banks are using to lend to small businesses. Maybe if they did not have such a good lender in the federal government there
April 28, 1993

would be more money available for small businesses. I am talking about interest rates here.
EIow can the hon. member stand up in this House and complain? I know the member and I think he is a good member for a Liberal. He is concerned about his concitoyens in this country and small business. He cares about the economic prospects of his constituents and other Canadians just as I do.
He must accept the fact that we have to pay for this deficit because we pay interest on that debt. We know what the impact of this is on interest rates. One does not have to be a rocket scientist to figure it out. If all the money required to finance government activities is used to pay interest on the deficit then it leaves much less in the coffer for those institutions to lend to the private sector and to small businesses and it drives the cost up.
We need a Small Businesses Loans Act to create incentives for those institutions to help the private sector and the small businesses grow.
How can they on the one hand want to have that capital accessible to the private sector and small business and at the same time in a consistent way oppose every measure proposed by this government to try to reduce and eliminate this deficit? How can they do that? How can they argue that we should have such an economic climate because he may want to rely on the Small Businesses Loans Act. I cannot wait for the day when we do not need the Small Businesses Loans Act and when the private sector and market forces will allow a business person in Canada with a good idea and product to go to the private sector market-a bank or financial institution-to get his or her loan. It makes sense to go ahead and succeed. That is what I would want.
However, before we get there we are going to have to pay our way as Canadians and that means we must stop borrowing to do everything we do every day.
We are now borrowing to pay the interest on the debt. When one gets to that point one has a serious problem. Now the Minister of Linance has put in the window a fiscal framework that sees Canada without a borrowing requirement of .9 per cent by the end of this fiscal framework.
The Budget
I think if we want to help small business then it is by what the Minister of Linance has shown us.

It is all right to try to score political points on the misery of people. However, what we are proposing to Canadians is not magic or an instant solution as with the Liberals where they spend more of the taxpayers' money and increase the deficit. Tax people. That is their way.
This is what we believe. To really help Canadians one must have the fundamentals right and in place. That is what we have been striving to do. Canada is poised for recovery like never before.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in this very quiet debate this afternoon. There is a friendly discussion going on.
I rise today to make a few comments about this budget that I feel is a terrible effort at financial management by this government. This is another long string of inept fiscal and other measures that have been pushed upon Canadians by this present government. It is a measure of ineptitude which fortunately we will soon have an opportunity to change.
The Budget
We have endured incredible hype about this budget in the past number of weeks as story after story circulated about the Draconian cuts that would be coming. Of course it is the classic manoeuvre of governments in the pre-election period to heighten the worst expectations and then try to show the voters what good people you really are.
In this case the government has not succeeded. The people have not been fooled and they will soon be able to pass judgment upon this government.
Thankfully, this is the last budget this government will bring down. It makes this an opportune time to review the government's record with regard to its fiscal management and forecasting ability.
This government has paid lip service to the concept of deficit reduction ever since it was elected. What we have seen, however, is not debt reduction but a massive increase in the public debt which now stands at record levels.
The promises of this government have never been matched by performance and we have no reason to believe its forecasting ability is going to improve at this late date.
The present finance minister missed on his projections not by thousands, not by millions, but by billions of dollars. There has been a mistake of $1.1 billion since December. He now tells us that the deficit in the coming year will be $35.5 billion. How do we know if this is correct? What is there in the government or the minister's track record that could possibly inspire any confidence?
Let us examine how we have arrived at where we are today. Jobs, jobs, jobs was the cry of the present Prime Minister before he was first elected. Jobs as a result of free trade was the promise in 1988. Deficit reduction was a priority throughout the past nine years. We now have the sad spectacle of the Minister of Finance of a government that made jobs, jobs, jobs its rallying ciy standing before this House and saying, in effect, that an unemployment rate of 10 per cent is quite acceptable and will continue in double digits into the foreseeable future.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
What does the future hold? I believe the government does not know. It does know how to attack hard-working Canadians and has gone out of its way to create a two-class system in this country: the rich and the poor. Sadly enough, during these past nine years the government has put middle-class Canada in a vice and slowly tightened the grip, forcing a wedge between the haves and the have-nots. This action is reprehensible and the government will feel the result of it in the near future.
Since the day it was elected this government has applied a double standard to the governing of this country. The Prime Minister at the outset appointed a huge cabinet to make sure as many MPs as possible shared in the spoils of victory. He appointed extra senators to impose an unpopular tax on Canadians and raised the art of patronage appointments to a new high.
On the other hand this government provoked a bitter strike with some of its lowest paid workers and now attempts to justify further slash and burn tactics by blaming government employees and programs for its financial ineptitude. The fact is that the economy has shrunk because of the government's mismanagement and therefore the deficit continues to grow.
To me, this is a government at war with itself. It is still talking and acting as if it was an opposition party. The Conservatives have been in power for almost nine years. It is their policies that have failed this countiy. It is their policies that have prolonged the recession so it now rivals the Great Depression of the 1930s. They must take the blame.
There are now food banks in every major city in Canada, more Canadians are living below the poverty line than ever before and the government has stood idly by and watched this happen. The institutions which have bound this countiy together have been destroyed and what was once an open and generous society has been threatened.
The government has also turned on the poorer regions of this country and is, in essence, cutting them off. It was noted in this House yesterday that the VIA Rail cuts will soon mean that only the corridor from Quebec City to Windsor will be serviced by passenger trains.
This is only a surface symptom of what is happening. Can you imagine how the people in my region where unemployment reaches 20 per cent feel when they hear that regional and industrial development will be cut and funding through ACOA will be cut by 25 per cent over the next few years?
We have just lived through this government's mismanagement of the fisheries and its total failure to act on behalf of the Canadian potato producers during the devastating PVY-N crisis and now we are told that more cuts are coming.
My province of Prince Edward Island will be the first affected by cutting the forestry agreement.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on a point of order. I wish to apologize to the hon. member for Hillsborough.
I would like to formally designate Thursday, April 29 as the second allotted day for this supply period.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I stated, my province of Prince Edward Island is the first that will be affected by the cutting of the forestry agreement. A one-year extension of the current federal-provincial forestry agreement which expired March 31 has gone up in smoke.
If I might for a moment quote Prince Edward Island's minister of agriculture, Walter Bradley, he said:
This announcement was completely unexpected, officials of both levels of government were in the process of finalizing priorities on a work plan for the coming year.
He went on to say that the non-renewal of the agreement will cost 250 direct jobs. He further stated:
The unilateral announcement by the federal government will impose serious hardship on wood lot owners, sawmill operators, and silviculture workers, not to mention the economic and environmental impact on the province.
These figures may not seem big to a government which is oriented toward big business and multinational corporations but they are significant numbers in a small province like mine. This government still has not learned after nine years in office that it is there to serve all Canadians of all social and economic levels and not just the big interests and the stronger members of our Canadian family.
April 28, 1993

It is interesting to note that despite the fact the government feels it has to close down a large segment of the forestry industry in Prince Edward Island it has chosen to leave the golden helicopter deal intact in an obvious ploy to help the leadership aspirations of the Minister of National Defence. We may not be able to afford pilots but we will have the choicest helicopters that money can buy.
The minister may have thought he was delivering a message of hope when he read his budget speech. What he did say was that he hopes things will get better. There is a distinct difference. He presented a budget that he said would restore confidence in Canada. Instead, the dollar has dropped even more as his friends in the financial markets have passed harsh judgment on his performance and that of his government.
This is a pre-election budget with no clear direction and no blueprint for the future. Our young people are facing another summer with few employment prospects. There is no job creation program for youth or for those millions of other Canadians who are out of work.
There is no clear plan to improve Canada's infrastructure. There is a lot of the minister's hope that things will get better and his wish that the economy will improve. He dreams that private businesses, at least those that have not moved, will be able to turn the economy around. Obviously he has given up trying himself.
The people of Canada will soon have the opportunity to pass judgment on this budget and on the nine years of this government's rule. They will remember nine years of a government saying one thing and doing another. This government talks of restraint and deficit reduction yet the deficit has increased beyond our wildest fears. It talked of jobs, jobs, jobs, yet joblessness is at an all-time high.
It talked of tax reform yet the goods and services tax has failed to make even a dent in the deficit, while at the same time causing Canadians undue hardship every day.
The government has managed the economy of this country with ineptitude and incompetence. It is my hope that when it is gone others will be able to pick up the pieces and return Canada to some of the glory it has seen in the past.
The Budget
The fortunate thing about this budget is that people will not have time to forget it before they go to the polls. The government's fear of the electorate has forced it into a corner and it must face the judgment of Canadians soon.
I believe that judgment will be harsh, and deservedly so. This government has done much harm to this country. This is a bad budget and I urge my fellow members to vote against it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly have spoken on budgets before in this House, although perhaps not on the budget debate but often on the borrowing bill the government normally introduces subsequent to a budget.
This year we had the borrowing bill first because the government was so disorganized it could not make up its mind about what to put in a budget. Having seen the one it produced the other day we can understand why. There is a complete lack of any ideas on the part of the government to try to ameliorate the economic situation it has created in this country and which has brought ruin to thousands and thousands of Canadians.
We have had record bankruptcies for the last few years, thanks to the government. We have had record unemployment for the last few years, thanks to the government. The Minister of Finance and his cabinet colleagues have really made a terrible mess of the finances of Canada. That is not unusual in my own experience because the last time we had a government that made such a mess of the national finances was the Diefenbaker government in the 1950s and early 1960s. I can still remember the clean-up job the Liberal Party had to do when it took office after defeating the Diefenbaker government in 1962.1 will not dwell on that today.
What I wanted to talk about was the fraud that is being perpetrated on the Canadian public by the Minister of Finance and the government in the budget that has been presented. We have got this very fancy little booklet that the government has produced en masse for people to read and it is full of statements that are utterly misleading and false.
I would like to quote one of the statements the minister had the nerve to read in the House during the

April 28, 1993
The Budget
course of his budget speech. It was so patently false I was amazed. If he had been on oath he would have been accused of perjury. He said: "Less borrowing, lower taxes, more jobs and more choice. That is the direction in which people want to go and that is the direction in which this government is going". He was all wrapped up in these words.
Let us look at the record, let us look at the facts that back up that statement. First of all, he said less borrowing. The deficit has increased for the last four or five years. It has gone up consistently every time and the minister says there is less borrowing. Where? Who is borrowing less as a result of this government's economic mismanagement? Certainly not the Government of Canada and certainly not the people of Canada who are having to pay the interest on the public debt. The less borrowing statement is patently false.
He said lower taxes. Where are the lower taxes? He told us there were no tax increases in this budget. That statement is also false because taxes are going up in this country because of the deindexation of deductions which this government has done in its past budgets. The government knows it is going to get more money this year as a result of the removal of the indexation provisions on all the deductions in the Income Ihx Act and the removal of the indexation on the rates of tax on various levels of income. Those have all been taken out, so taxes will go up this year.
The government says there are no tax increases. There are not any in this budget but there are tax increases coming into place as a result of previous budgets. We have had something like 35 tax increases in the last eight years already. He said lower taxes are what Canadians want. If they are what they want and that is the direction in which the government is going, where are the tax decreases? Where are the lower taxes? There were none in this budget.
Then he said there are more jobs. Where are the job creation schemes in this budget? There are not any. The government announced with some pride that it was laying off 16,000 public servants. The President of the Treasury Board spoke in the House yesterday and shed crocodile tears at this loss, but he is party to the government that is doing this. He is letting these people go-
The minister said this is job creation, more jobs. What is it? Is it job loss or job creation? Why does the minister not tell us? Why does the Minister of Finance not tell the truth to Canadians instead of these falsehoods? Why does he not tell them that there are not more jobs but fewer jobs as a result of this budget. It is a do-nothing budget. It is worse than do-nothing. It is damaging to the Canadian economy.
Then he said more choice. I do not know what he meant by that. I do not think he did either. I think he ran out of words with more in front of them. He had to think of words that he could put more in front of to make it sound as though something was better. He stuck in the word choice. I do not know what choice he meant. If he meant that one has more places one can go for help from the government that is false because it is closing offices right, left and centre in an effort to save money. The government makes us make these long distance telephone calls that cost more and tie up Canadians more in their efforts to get answers from the government. There is not more choice. There is less.
He said this is the direction the government is going in. I would like to know where he got that idea. I suspect somebody, some Tory hack in his office, wrote that statement and stuck it in because I notice it is on all the little budget summaries the government is handing out, the one card deal. I notice that is on there in heavy print almost word for word, though not quite the same. I suppose he said it in different places in different ways, but it quotes him as having said it that way on April 26. That is something that is wrong.
The other thing I wanted to refer to was the minister's incredible statements about the reduction of the deficit. Every year for nine years we have heard about deficit reduction in Canada. It is always just around the comer. We remember the former Minister of Finance, the member for Etobicoke Centre. He is long gone from that job and everybody has forgotten him. He used to talk about holding the course. He used to say that we are going to hold the course. We did not hear that expression in the budget the other day, did we?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what the Titanic did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is like the Titanic, but he did not use the expression. I guess the Minister of Finance realized that being in charge of the Titanic one ought not hold the
April 28, 1993

course. Maybe he has realized that the ship of state he has been running on icebergs for the last few years is really coming to ground. He did not use it.
We did not hear about the fundamentals either. We used to hear how we always had the fundamentals right.
I do not think the government ever knew what the fundamentals were, let alone whether it got them right or not. It has them all wrong. Everything is wrong in this budget.
Let us go back to these figures on deficit reduction. This is an unbelievable set of statements. The government says that its budgetary deficit this year will be $35 billion. This is the fourth or fifth straight increase in the deficit. Every year the government says it is reducing the deficit, it has control, it has the fundamentals right, it is doing everything right and everything is working. Yet the deficit has gone up again for the fourth or fifth year. The projections are that it will go down next year and the year after that until in 1996-97 it will be down to $14 billion, according to page 62 of the minister's budget.
He has nothing in here to back that up. The minister has the credibility of Mother Goose.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I'll tell him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell him. I urge the President of the Treasury Board to go and tell him and get out his Mother Goose books to see if they have any more credibility than this budget document. It is absolutely unbelievable. I have here an old budget just to prove my point. It is dated November 8,1984, and is from the former Minister of Finance, the member for Etobicoke Centre. It was not actually a budget but an economic statement. This was his first effort.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was one of those last December.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was not the first economic statement but it was the first Tory economic statement in a number of years. The Tories told us that with their projections everything was just going to be terrible because of the awful state of affairs they inherited from the previous government. They went on and on about that for pages and pages. I quote from page 97 of Hansard from November 8. He said:
With this set of projections-the deficit for this fiscal year would
be $34.5 billion, almost $5 billion higher than projected last
The Budget
February by the previous government. That is bad enough but that is not the worst of it. Current projections show the deficit increasing next year to more than $37 billion and remaining between $34 and $38 billion in every year for the balance of this decade.
That was to take us up to 1990. Remember he was talking in 1984. He continued:
This is in marked contrast to previous projections that showed the deficit declining over that period.
The former Minister of Finance was very upset about these projections and he decided he had better do something about it. He said he would take action, and so he did. He took action and introduced all kinds of tax breaks for his wealthy friends and various other benefits that he said were going to help solve this problem. Of course they did not. He said:
But move we must.
This is from page 100, so we can see how long he went on about this stuff. He said:
Our goal is to reduce the projected level of annual expenditures by 1990 by $10 to $15 billion, inclusive of the measures I am announcing tonight.
He already had other cuts but we know that the expenditures did not decline by $10 billion or $15 billion by 1990. They never got down anywhere near that far. Now they have gone up by a lot more than that, and those were good times. They were growth years, record growth years. One would have thought the minister could have salted away a bit of money for the rainy day the way Conservatives are always saying we have to do. They always blame the Liberals in Ontario for not salting away enough money for the rainy day. Now we hear the same song and dance from the socialists.
That is what the minister did, and of course his deficit projections were all wrong. If those figures were accurate I think we would find that the deficit by 1990 would be down to about $15 billion. It never got anywhere close to $15 billion in 1990 or any other time since this government took office. It has always stayed in the $30 billion range. It has never been able to get out of this, and now it is up as high as $35 billion.
We had these awful projections that if something was not done the debt was going to be something like $415 billion by 1990. It is way over that. It is going to be $500 billion very shortly according to the minister's own projections and his own budget that he introduced.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
The national debt will hit $500 billion in early 1994. This was considered a national catastrophe in 1984. For that reason the Tory government said it was going to take action, solve that problem and make things work. Every year in every budget it has told us that the actions it was taking were saving us billions of dollars and it was going to solve this deficit problem. Yesterday was the latest example and now the deficit is worse than ever before. This government is hopeless. It cannot organize anything. Its projections have the credibility of Mother Goose.
The Minister of Finance should withdraw this budget. He should get out of office and call an election. He is incompetent and the whole government is incompetent to govern this country. It has made a terrible, terrible mess of it. Even Jeff Simpson in The Globe and Mail wrote an article entitled "From a tired government, a budget without inspiration or conviction".
Everybody knows this is a tired old broken down Tory government that is breaking the whole country down by hanging on to office. My colleague from Hamilton West says he cannot withdraw because there is a leadership campaign. Call an election anyway. Let the people make a decision. We do not need a new leader in the Tory Party. Putting a new label on the old bottle will not do any good.
There are two things that we have suggested that I would like to draw to the minister's attention as something he could have done to improve this mess.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in what my colleague from Kingston and the Islands has to contribute to this debate. As we are dealing here with the budget, I am most interested in his suggestion that we tell the Minister of Finance to just withdraw his budget, resign his job and let us get on with an election.
I wonder if he can really do that because what he was really doing was probably giving us a pre-leadership budget. Really, what can the Minister of Finance do when Campbell and Charest are running against each other?
Maybe the member for Kingston and the Islands can explain this to me, but as I recall was it not Campbell who said the deficit was going to-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Again I have to say to the hon. member that he is speaking of the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment. Please.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will respect that wish of the Chair. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for correcting me. I just wanted to make it clear to my constituents who I was referring to. They may not follow all these positions quite as closely as the member for Kingston and the Islands and I do. They change so often who can keep track?
The Minister of National Defence told us we could get rid of that deficit-and the member for Lincoln can tell me as I think she is co-chairing her campaign-in five years, I believe. We are not going to have a deficit any more after five years. Then the Minister of the Environment said we can get rid of it in four years. As a result we are going to end up with individuals who can produce plans for us that say we will not even have a deficit.
Now wait a minute. The Minister of Finance gave us a budget that said we are going to be about $8 billion- It is five minutes for questions and comments, right, Mr. Speaker? I am taking a couple of minutes just to ask my question. I will cut off now so I can listen to my colleague from Kingston and the Islands who may explain this pre-leadership budget which could develop into a preelection budget in another month or so.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands will have at least one minute.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be pleased to respond to my very distinguished colleague from Hamilton West as quickly as I can.
It is clear that the Minister of National Defence thinks the deficit can be solved in five years and I think the Minister of the Environment said four years. They are influential ministers in this cabinet so one would think that in the years they have been there they might have done something to bring this about. But clearly the deficit has gone up and not down with them in the cabinet. They have been utterly useless as far as deficit reduction is concerned. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs has done more to reduce the deficit
April 28, 1993

than either the Minister of the Environment or the Minister of National Defence. I think neither of them has any idea how to solve the problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, she is not flying first class anymore.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And unfortunately she is leaving public office. They are losing the people who could help and they are gaining-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret that the hon. member's time has expired. I really regret that because he always comes up with a very good speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to follow the member opposite who is certainly quite capable of telling many nursery stories. I was amazed at his presentation because he seemed to have such a strong interest in reducing the deficit and yet his party's policy on that particular issue is so vacuous.
I understand that his leader has announced he wants to reduce the deficit to $25 billion. That of course would mean that the debt would continue to rise. Our policy is to reduce it to less than 1 per cent of the gross domestic product by 1997.
Clearly the opposition members of both parties are only interested in spending and continuing to spend. The level of restraint that has been indicated in this particular budget is certainly far beyond anything they are considering.
The only party in Canada aside from our party that is prepared to tackle the deficit is the Reform Party and I think its method of tackling the deficit is just unacceptable to Canadians.
I feel very confident about what Canadians think. I participated in this budget process and I consulted my constituents. I sent them out a "You Be the Finance Minister" pamphlet that many of them took the opportunity to fill out. Many of them went through this exercise and a vast overwhelming number balanced the budget.
