The Budget
My people are going to be very disappointed that the finance minister did not cut further. I was initially quite disappointed but in considering it I think we are quite right, this is a pre-leadership budget. Certainly this is going to be the main issue in the next election. I am absolutely confident that the vast majority of Canadians want to see the deficit cut further. They want to see the national debt paid down.
The only programs that my constituents wanted to increase or remain the same were health and welfare, the environment and agriculture. With respect to transfers to persons they cut everything but seniors' benefits. Transfers to the provinces, health, education and job creation were the only things they did not want to cut.
It is clear to me that the finance minister followed the wishes of my constituents and Canadians across this country. He cut everywhere they suggested with the following exceptions. He did not cut other transfers to persons. My constituents were not aware who these other persons were. I am sure they would not want to cut funding to veterans or the disabled.
Similarly he did not cut payments to less wealthy provinces, the EPF funding and the CAP. As he has stated this has to be negotiated with the provinces. It has to be done together. These programs are too important and clearly my constituents want health and welfare to remain. They wanted cuts made to the Canada Assistance Plan but I think we must all agree in this House that the least able Canadians must be helped and that must be treated in a very sensitive fashion.
Similarly the minister did not cut funding to Indians and Inuit. All of the other areas that my constituents wanted to cut were in fact cut and those they did not want cut were not cut.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wow, that is great.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the member is quite right. This is a pre-leadership budget and an election is imminent. There is no new legislation possible so the finance minister had a dilemma. The problem in the 1992-93 budget was that the revenues anticipated did not appear. Spending is under control. This government has a very tight control over spending in this country.
The problem was the revenues and some of that can be addressed administratively looking at some of the slip-

April 28, 1993
The Budget
page. For the rest of it we have to have an improved economy. In looking at this budget he had to balance the two objectives of restraining spending and controlling the deficit as well as stimulating the economy.
He needed something credible and achievable that was sensitive to the public's wishes. He was also constrained because he could not touch $41 billion in debt payments. The programs he did not touch cost about $52 billion and the debt payments are $41 billion. That meant only about $60 billion worth of expenditures could be tackled and over the five-year period that section of government spending will be cut by $30 billion.
The 1993-94 cut is $3.8 billion rising to $5.8 billion in 1994-95. Those are very substantial cuts given the fact that these departments have been under restraints since 1984 and the demands of the population are not diminishing. It is going to be a tremendous challenge to those departments to maintain the quality of services that Canadians are used to.
We had a remark earlier by one of the members about a particular incident that occurred in Toronto. My office was also flooded with calls. The fact is that was not a reduction in service at all. There was a major computer error and a lot of papers went out that were inaccurate. They were followed very quickly by a second series of computer runs. The elderly people were very confused. These were the statements regarding their OAS benefits.
At the same time another office was transferring to a different location so calls were being rerouted to the Toronto office and the phone lines were jammed. I think that is very peculiar. Usually my office finds that the Department of National Health and Welfare does respond. We do occasionally have to intervene but we are able to get through and resolve those problems. I think there will be a real challenge.
We also deal with immigration a lot in my particular office. I am pleased with the new measures which will result in greater efficiency and greater uniformity in the treatment of people. The calls will be centralized to one location. Of course there will be reductions in the cost. A 1-800 number is going to be open for a much more extended period of time with a whole bank of switchboard operators and a computerized system where people will be able to access information quickly. It is going to be a tremendous improvement.
We have had to deal with many immigration inquiries and I think that by centralizing and upgrading the service tremendous amounts of money will be saved. The total amount of savings in the immigration budget is $1 billion. The legislation that went through will result in that. That is something my constituents are very much in favour of.
I think the minister has presented a very realistic attempt to continue on course at this time. It is a thoughtful and strategic approach that will help Canadians compete and help our economy grow. It will help to drag us out of our fiscal sink-hole.
The members opposite said there is nothing in the budget about jobs. I listened carefully to what my constituents were saying. I attended many of the prosperity sessions. The business community wants us to provide a stable economic environment. They want low inflation and low interest rates. That is what this budget is trying to do. They do not want new taxes. Many of the items in this budget will help them in terms of their business loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act and other measures will improve the taxation system for business. These are nitty-gritty things, the kind of things the Grits opposite never think about.
There are very real cuts in this budget. Those constraints on the departments will result in very real cuts. The departments will be challenged. They will have to come forward. I think we will have ministers delivering a succession of bills to accomplish those goals. There have been tremendous improvements. It will be a manageable means of cutting that will give proper consideration to various alternatives.
Certainly as far as the provinces are concerned we have to work together on those programs because the Canadian public value them. We have to talk about efficiencies in the health care system and in our social spending.
I think the Reform Party has been very aggressive. Many of my constituents who responded to my questionnaire are leaning toward the Reform Party because they are so deeply concerned about the deficit. However they clearly do not want the cuts that the Reform Party wants to make. One of their suggestions is to base the OAS tax-back on family income rather than individual income. My constituents oppose cuts to seniors' benefits, health, education, job training and agriculture. Shifting the tax back in that manner would mean that couples
April 28, 1993

would be very unfairly treated. Right now seniors receive their benefits based on individual income. Requiring women in a significant majority to lose their OAS benefit because their husbands have a high income I think would be most unacceptable to my constituents and indeed I think very unfair.
We have the tax back in place for those who are quite wealthy and who are not receiving the OAS. I think any further tampering with the seniors' benefits would have to be something that would be considered very carefully in conjunction with the seniors.
As a baby boomer I am concerned about what is going to happen to our benefits when we get to retirement age.
I do think that retirement benefits for seniors have to be looked at. I think we have to secure the retirement income of Canadians who have lived and worked in this country. That I think is an undertaking that our members are very concerned about as is the general public.
I have already mentioned that the Liberal target for the deficit is $20 billion to $25 billion. I think that is far away from what we are talking about. We are talking about eventually a zero deficit, but in terms of the five-year approach we are talking about it being 4.5 per cent in 1993 and .9 per cent by 1997. The Clinton budget in the U.S. has a target of 2.5 per cent by 1997.
Actually we have done a lot better than every other G-7 nation. When we look at our particular situation and the international statistics we have confronted a worldwide recession. The latest revised forecast from the IMF indicates that we are projected to lead the G-7 nations with respect to economic growth.
We have mortgages with the lowest interest rates in 35 years, inflation at the lowest level in 30 years, government spending at the lowest level in 33 years, productivity and unit costs that have gone down 6.6 per cent and the highest exports in history. In terms of managing this economy I think we are doing very well.
Obviously it is a very difficult period for many Canadians. However, when we actually look at the job statistics that have been churned out there has been a tremendous amount of movement. We have a very dynamic economy. There are new jobs being created and
The Budget
other jobs being lost. We are facing a revolution in terms of technology.
What is the answer to that? Is the answer to put up fences to attempt to control what is a natural occurrence in a dynamic economy or to tiy to help Canadians to adjust by giving them better training, better education and creating an environment that encourages businesses to expand and to locate in Canada?
We now have through the efforts of the finance minister the best tax regime in the world for research and development. I am proud of that. I think that is something business really wants.
Of course the Liberals have opposed every single cut that we brought forward and so has the NDP. The only cut that they would like to see that we would not like to see is the helicopters. This amount of money is $4.4 billion over 13 years in 1993 dollars. That averages $340 million per year. They have spent this at least 10 times over.
There are a number of people who are talking about day care versus helicopters. They say we should do this or do that and reduce the deficit. This would not make any kind of significant reduction in the deficit because it is too small. It is not even $1 billion. It is $340 million a year.
We know it is a tremendous boost to a great number of industries in Canada. In terms of job creation and retaining the kinds of jobs that we need to move into the future it is excellent.
It is something that the companies are now delivering, having receptions for and recognizing. I think more Canadians will realize that this is an expenditure that is important to Canada and a good way to create good long-term jobs.
The NDP of course offers a full employment strategy. As the chair of the poverty committee I have had a great deal to do with the NDP's full employment strategy. I have been trying to find out what it is for four years. We kept asking the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing for specific examples. We kept asking him to bring forward his suggestions. None were brought forward.

The Budget
I have however seen an NDP job strategy in Ontario. It has devastated Ontario. It is clearly something that is really smoke and mirrors in the strongest sense of the word. It has resulted in devastating consequences in Ontario. It has exacerbated the recession, scared the hell out of business and really contributed to the situation we are in currently. I am pleased however that Premier Rae seems to have learned a lot lately and is attempting at last to tackle some of the serious problems.
I attended a Conference Board session out west where I met with various leaders from across the country in the business sector, the government sector and the education sector. It was a very stimulating experience. Their concerns were much the same as the concerns of my constituents and I think that our government is certainly on the right track.
The Conference Board predicts that all Canadian governments will be constrained in spending for at least the next 10 years. I think we need to stop joking around in this Chamber and start looking at this in a serious fashion.
The challenge will be to make better use of scarce government dollars and yet treat Canadians fairly and allow these scarce government dollars to be given to those who need it most. That is exactly what we are trying to do at the poverty subcommittee. We have been examining the issue of poverty measures and the use thereof with a view to providing a means of identifying and monitoring the welfare of Canadians at the bottom end of our society so that governments will be held accountable and we can actually see whether or not programs have in fact worked.
We are looking at this situation and I think in terms of policy it will be extremely important. We do not now have a poverty line. Statistics Canada has repeatedly told people that the low-income cut-offs are not a poverty line and in fact they make a very poor poverty line.
I will mention one little item to illustrate what a poor poverty line they make. It includes taxes in the current numbers. If one takes taxes out one reduces the number of poor in Canada by 3 per cent. If one looks at the elderly population one reduces it even further. This is because under our taxes we transfer considerable amounts of income to low-income Canadians. Surely when we are looking at poverty in Canada we should be
considering the impact of what in fact we do through the tax and transfer system.
I have been accused of playing with the figures for the benefit of our party. The fact of the matter is that this is -historical data. The Liberal Party will be pleased to learn that it makes them look better too because many of the tax measures that were introduced were introduced under the Liberal Party. One can see the pattern that has occurred through the tax transfers.
However, in looking at poverty, we need national standards. The amount of money one needs to live in Toronto is not the same amount of money that one needs to live in Vancouver, Calgaiy, Winnipeg or Montreal. We know that through very accurate data now collected by Central Mortgage and Housing on every single community in Canada and Statistics Canada with respect to Agriculture Canada. There are tremendous variations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will the member tell us whether there is one person in Canada other than on her side of the House who has had anything positive to say about the budget? Second, I would like to know the name of the person or the organization.
We now have 10,000 people a month visiting our food bank in Edmonton. I am wondering if she has any thoughts of that in view of the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the budget all the international agencies that are used to monitor this sort of thing have given it very high ratings.
Those are delivered across Canada to businesses and so on. That is why we have seen stock market activity in this country that shows quite clearly that the business community has confidence in this government and not in any other group.
With respect to the food banks, Edmonton is in a province with welfare rates that are probably inadequate to cover basic necessities. I feel that food banks are a humiliating and degrading way to give people basic necessities.
I very strongly believe that we should have welfare rates in this country that are sufficient to cover basic needs such as food, clothing and shelter along with all the basic essentials.
April 28, 1993

I think we should work toward eliminating food banks. Indeed, when people working at the food banks appeared before our committee they said exactly the same thing. They want to eliminate the need for food banks.
I know that in Ontario and in Toronto in particular we had many discussions about this when I was on the community services and housing committee for 11 years. We attempted to get proper rent supplements and so on. We felt that the incomes of poor people should be sufficient to cover basic necessities.
There have always been agencies that have given out food. I think we have to talk about a system in which the self-esteem of people in low income situations is considered and they are helped in a very positive way. They should be given the basic essentials and also pathways out of poverty.
Our recommendation in the poverty subcommittee was for welfare to be at a basic needs level and for the child benefit to be on top to ensure an adequate discretionary income for children. I think those are very excellent goals.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak to the budget that was brought down by the Government of Canada on Monday of this week.
In listening to the last speaker in this House I am wondering if I am in the House of Commons of the right country. The words I have just heard do not reflect to any degree what I have to say about the budget that was brought down on Monday. They do not reflect the opinion that is widespread in my own constituency.
The motion we are debating is from the minister who wishes us to agree in general with his budget statement. I have to put on the record that I could not do that. Instead I would totally support the motion of non-confidence put forward by my own party which says that this House condemns the government for presenting a shopworn copy of last year's budget.
It fails to present a realistic and comprehensive program to create jobs and an economic recovery to permit the millions of Canadians whose lives have been crushed by Tory policies to regain their hope and livelihood.
This government fails to offer a credible and fair plan to control and reduce public debt. It fails to provide
The Budget
Canadians with a true and accurate account of the eight and a half years of Conservative government mismanagement.
This government is in serious trouble. This country is in serious trouble. The credit rating of this country is in doubt today. The markets are volatile.
Canadians, including constituents of mine in Northumberland are very concerned about the future of this country. They no longer feel that they live in the Canada they grew up in, that they prospered in, that offered them the opportunity of a bright future. Canadians do not know that vision of their country today. They long for it and hope it will return, that prosperity will return. However they were devastated with the budget as it was presented on Monday.
The most important fact is that the budget does nothing to get our economy moving forward again. We see a stand-pat budget, one that talks of further cuts, cuts into the future. It is a very safe budget for a government that is going into a federal election this year, a government that postpones to three years hence words about cuts. It has been promoting and selling to the Canadian people that the only policy and the only problem of any significance and any importance in this country is the debt and the deficit and the deficit in financial terms only.
People in this House recognize that the deficit and the debt are very serious problems and must be addressed, but this party would do something to help this economy recover. The economy must be helped to grow. The budget we were presented with on Monday does absolutely nothing to encourage that. Instead it deadens any spirit of optimism and hope people might have had.
During the tenure of this government Canadians have had their taxes raised 36 times. Consumer spending is presently down because of the fear experienced by Canadians. When members on the other side of the House speak it sounds like another country. Instead of a recovery however in my constituency there are still more and more jobs being lost as companies close and leave, as more and more people close up shop and go into bankruptcy. Just yesterday we heard of the difficulties of the Mack truck company. It is closing its doors and is purported to be moving south.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
The government says that we have an unemployment rate of around 11 per cent and that we have to expect that to continue well into 1994. In the constituency of Northumberland that is not a believable figure. A census was done in a neighbouring township to my riding of Northumberland. It was found that in fact the unemployment level was 14.6 per cent. Over 6 per cent of the population said that they were grossly underpaid. They were working but did not derive enough income to support themselves in any lifestyle that way not just survival.
Recovery in this country with no jobs is no recovery. We must have a recovery that provides jobs for Canadians. We have over one million people unemployed in Canada and the government wants to know what the Liberal Party would do that is different. We would create wealth in this country. We would put people back to work. If we put one million people back to work we would save $20 billion and that would go a long way to reducing the deficit.
In the budget we heard the finance minister talk about what was going to occur in Canada next year, the year after that and five years hence. So many of the things he said were just absolutely unbelievable. If we consider his prognostications about the deficit itself, it is interesting to look back to last year where in his budget speech of February 1992 he said that the deficit for 1992-93 would be $27.5 billion. In December he changed his mind. He regretted that his prognostication was out and that it would rise to $34.4 billion. Monday he said that since December he had to change his mind again and that now the deficit was going to be $35.5 billion. That is a difference of $8 billion in his prognostications for one year, the year we have just gone through.
How can we possibly believe a finance minister who says that in the year 1997-98 our deficit will be only $8 billion? In 1988 the deficit for 1992 was to be $19.5 billion. Monday it was changed to $35.5 billion.
This government has no credibility whatsoever and it is very obvious in all of the economic measures it has brought down, which I believe we have debated against very honestly and forthrightly. We have tried to point out the problems with the cuts, cuts, cuts this government has brought forward. We have tried to show that they were not good for this country. Obviously the government has not come up to its own predictions about its
policies. It is way off track which is not just causing a lot of consternation for individuals in Canada but for people around the world.
The Liberals would follow a two-track policy for economic recovery in this country. One track would deal very specifically with the deficit and the debt, knowing that those are very serious problems. There must be expenditure reductions by streamlining processes and eliminating duplication, while continuing to deliver the basic services that Canadians need. This must take place in consultation with the provinces.
We have done an analysis in doing some economic union work with the western provinces. We have shown that in one year, if we could do our government purchasing together, work more efficiently together, we could save $5 billion. Working more efficiently and streamlining our systems and processes does not mean cutting, it means saving billions of dollars.
Our government would also do many things to foster economic growth, investing in people, investing in research and development and infrastructure. People must be put back to work so that they are paying taxes rather than collecting unemployment insurance or welfare payments. As I said before, we have to remember that one million Canadians are unemployed and that is costing our country $20 billion a year.
To my mind the deficit that is more important than the financial deficit is the human deficit. We can work with monetary policies to reduce the deficit and we will do so. But the human deficit is going to be long term and will be very hard to cope with.
I recommend to everybody the report put out by the Senate Standing Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology in January 1991, which talks very clearly about the long-term negative effects of poverty on people in Canada. We know that the joblessness and consequent poverty in this country have been very much responsible for family breakdowns, stress, abuse against women and children, violence and crime, the breakdown of society. We need to get Canadians back to work and this budget is no solution to that end.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about a government that has set itself a priority. The priority this government has set itself is the reduction of the deficit, the reduction of the national debt. That is the yearly amount of money we spend and the collection of all those different years of budgets.
April 28, 1993

The Minister of Finance should take a moment to walk in his riding. I invite him to come to my riding of Hamilton West. If he were to sit in the local coffee shop or to take a walk around the downtown market or streets for just a few minutes, he would quickly realize that he has his priorities wrong, that the Tory Party has its priorities wrong.
That is because most people today are talking about jobs: "Give me a job. Give me the opportunity of a job". Then everything else will look after itself and we will not have to worry about whether there is enough money in the kitty to pay for social services. We will not have to worry whether there is enough welfare money in the kitty.
My constituents are telling me: "Stan, get into the House of Commons and will you just repeat it again and again and maybe, just maybe one of the new leadership candidates will understand that the priority in this country ought to be jobs. Let us create jobs".
When was the last time we heard about jobs from this government? Well, as many of my colleagues have already said, it was in 1984. The Prime Minister of this great country said: "My priority is jobs, jobs, jobs". That is a direct quote.
What do we have? Today we have 1.6 million people who are unemployed and over three million who are underemployed. That means people with some kind of a job, part-time jobs here or there, who really want to be employed full-time but cannot because the jobs just are not there. What do we have? We have around four million people who are unemployed or underemployed.
I ask my constituents this simple question: Are you any better off today than you were in 1988? Are you any better off today than you were back in 1984 when this government took office? Chances are you are going to say that you are not. How can we not be when we are in the greatest country in the world, Canada? With all our opportunities, with all our advancements in education, with all our natural resources, we sit here with close to four million people either out of work or looking for full-time jobs. Horrible, it is just horrible.
The Budget
My constituents would have something to say about it if I did not get specific with this government about the problems in Hamilton West. In Hamilton West the unemployment rate is higher than the national unemployment rate which is 11 per cent. In Hamilton it is 11.7 per cent. Hamilton has 38,000 people unemployed. It is inexcusable.
Let me talk about youth unemployment. Hamilton West and the city of Hamilton and area is proud to have McMaster University, which is one of the major employers in our area. Youth unemployment in Hamilton is at 19 per cent. Nineteen per cent of students cannot find jobs.
Let us jump over to bankruptcies in Hamilton. We are talking about consumer and business bankruptcies. In 1988 there were 508 consumer bankruptcies and 102 business bankruptcies. In 1992 that number has jumped to 1,504 personal bankruptcies and 201 business bankruptcies.
I do not have to convince my constituents in Hamilton West of that. We all walk around downtown. We see how many stores in Jackson Square have masking tape over the glass. They are all shut down. It is now free rent for a few of the stores still there that use it for storage space next door. It is a horrible situation.
Regarding welfare statistics, the case-load in Hamilton has increased since 1990. In November 1990 the general welfare assistance case-load stood at 9,836. By March 1993, just last month, the case-load for general welfare assistance was 17,011. That is an increase of over 40 per cent.
But this government keeps telling us: "Stay the course. We know where we are going. We are going to build on what we have in this country". What we have in this country is a hell of a mess. There are people looking for work. We have to create the jobs.
Like all the budgets of the Tory government since 1984, this budget provides no hope for Canadians and it is filled with the usual empty rhetoric. Most of all it is laden with all those unrealistic projections. The budget is silent on a whole range of issues including, tragically, solutions for the 1.6 million Canadians who are unemployed and the over three million Canadians who are underemployed or have part-time work and are looking for full-time jobs.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
Not only did this government promise jobs, jobs, jobs back in 1984 but it also promised the most generous retraining programs for workers laid off because of that Mulroney trade deal back in 1988. I have to be honest. There were more than a few friends of mine in Hamilton West who said the trade deal had a chance and they were going to vote Conservative because it just might be the ticket. Part of the reason they did so was that this government promised them "the most generous retraining programs this country has ever seen". Those were the words of the Prime Minister.
Have they developed? There are constituents sitting in Hamilton West today who had good jobs, a wife, children, a mortgage and maybe even a cottage or a boat. Tragically eight years later some of my constituents who were married are no longer married. They are divorced. They no longer hold a mortgage because they cannot afford to pay the mortgage. They no longer have the luxury of a cottage or a boat. That went long before the mortgage went.
This was because of the stress put upon them by the inability to have a job that was not there. The government promised they would be retrained. They lost their jobs because of the free trade agreement. They lost their jobs because that company went south. They did not get retrained. They could not get retrained. There was nothing to be retrained for and if they could be retrained this government was not going to help them get retrained.
Ten minutes go very quickly. I will conclude my remarks in the same manner in which I began, with a question. Why did we have this budget in the first place, if that is what we call a budget? It is a total failure. In the end how does it all matter? It is another tired piece of guesswork from a lame duck government which within just a handful of months will not have the mandate to carry through with any of it.
Canadians are the lucky ones. After all, this is a pre-leadership budget that may be discarded anyway in the next couple of months to make room for a pre-election budget which probably will be brought in by the minister of defence, the Minister of the Environment or whoever wins that leadership contest. God knows that this thing called a budget lacks the economic plan to
produce R and D, training and most of all jobs to turn this country around, to instil a new confidence in the Canadian people. That is what a budget has to do. That is what this budget did not do.
The Prime Minister and the finance minister should hear the people when they say: "Give me a job. Give me the retraining that is needed for that job". Everything else will look after itself.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and to Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance on Monday.
First of all, I would like to congratulate the minister on his realistic approach to the difficult choices he had to make. In this budget the government is staying the course set in 1984 with a view to reducing the deficit and, within a reasonable period of time, to eliminating it altogether.
As we have said repeatedly, these difficult decisions must be made and implemented now because the deficit, and especially the interest on the debt it generates prevents us from introducing new social measures.
A government's budget at whatever level is no different from a family budget. Of course there is a difference in scale and complexity, but in both cases, if we continue to spend more than we earn, we are soon faced with a crisis.
We all know there are not umpteen ways to cut the deficit. We either increase revenues or cut spending. Increasing revenues would have meant increasing taxes. The Minister of Finance wisely preferred to cut departmental spending.
Canadians already bear a heavy tax burden, and announcing new tax increases would have had a disastrous impact on the economic recovery.
Both business and individuals pay their fair share of taxes, and I think their resources are stretched to the limit. Raising taxes would have been the easy way out but unrealistic in the circumstances. That is why the Minister of Finance preferred to make further cuts in government operations and departmental spending.
April 28, 1993

Like any business faced with revenue shortfalls the government has decided to cut operating costs and program spending. For instance, the federal Public Service, where the number of positions has already been cut by 90,000, will be expected to reduce the number of public servants by about 16,500 over the next five years. However, despite these cutbacks the government's intentions are clear. It wants to do, and will do, everything in its power to prevent any reduction in services to the public.
As the Minister of Finance pointed out, and I quote: "The government will continue to streamline its operations and improve the cost-effectiveness of its service delivery. We will make government smaller, simpler and more accessible to Canadians."
I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate members of the federal Public Service on the excellent way they are doing their jobs. They are all doing everything they can to help us improve the way government responds to the needs of the public and they have every reason to be proud of their record. It will not be easy for them to manage these new cutbacks, but we are asking them to co-operate because they must realize that the government has no choice and that as responsible administrators we must stay the course on reducing the deficit.
They will all have a major role to play in this process, and I am convinced we will again be able to rely on their efficiency, competence and dedication to help us in this difficult task.
As part of its policy to cut costs and improve service to the public, a commitment made in 1984 and reiterated subsequently, the government has adopted a number of measures aimed at simplifying communication between business, individuals and government. For instance, the minister announced a simplified GST system for small business. I am referring to improvements in the quick method for computing GST which would simplify procedures for hundreds of thousands of small businesses.
These are not necessarily headline grabbers, but based on my conversations with business people, I can assure you these measures are most welcome because while reducing the cost of government operations they also reduce administration costs of Canadian businesses.
The Budget
Less paper burden means businesses have more time and money to spend on improving and expanding their operations.
These are very simple little measures that have a big impact, directly and indirectly, on the cost of management for our Canadian businessmen and women.
We must also be pleased that social programs were not affected by the announced cuts. In fact, aid for seniors, the program for the disabled, veterans' pensions and benefits, some programs for native people, the national employment strategy and famine relief in the world are all exempt from restrictions.
We thus ensure that those most in need will not be penalized and I think that is a very wise choice, because in these difficult economic times, it would be irresponsible to cut more from the resources for the most disadvantaged. More than anyone, they feel the impact of Canada's financial difficulties. Someone earning $60,000 a year can support a $10 cut, but for someone living below the poverty line, this same $10 cut has frightful consequences.
We must clearly understand that Canada's financial situation cannot be seen in isolation. Canada is strongly influenced by the world situation. In this increasingly international world in which we live, when the market economies are more and more interdependent, we benefit when the world economy is well but we suffer when it is doing badly.
There is no use hiding our head in the sand. For several years we have been living through a worldwide recession which Canada, as a major industrialized country, could not escape. However because of the spin off benefits generated from the wide range of initiatives for economic renewal taken by this government since 1984 the Canadian economy is improving and is in a very good position to perform well in the coming years.
For example, according to the OECD's predictions Canada will have the highest growth rate of the G-7 countries this year and next. In the past few months we have witnessed an encouraging turnaround in economic growth, employment, retail sales and several other important indicators. The most vigorous growth was in

April 28, 1993
The Budget
our exports which are mainly responsible for the economic recovery.
Strong exports were made possible by a spectacular improvement in our cost competitiveness as well as greater access to the American market under the free trade agreement. This strong performance of our exports will continue to support the economic recovery in 1993-94.
As I said earlier, Canada either benefits or suffers from the global economic situation, but we must also promote trade and encourage policy harmonization on the domestic market.
If the federal, provincial and territorial governments shoot in all directions chances are that nothing great will come out of it. That is why I again applaud the Minister Finance's commitment to working and co-operating with his provincial counterparts.
The money comes from only one source the taxpayer. That is why it is essential that a national cure be found for the national debt problem, as Canadians want. In that sense the federal and provincial governments must work together toward achieving this goal. If the federal government reduces its debt at the expense of the provinces that solves nothing. It simply shifts the taxpayers' burden from one level of government to another. That is simply juggling the books.
Knowing that, the Minister of Finance preferred to play it straight by not cutting provincial transfers, a decision applauded by the provincial finance ministers, including the Quebec finance minister, Gerard D. Levesque. After the federal budget was tabled, he said: "The federal minister is tackling the deficit with measures that will benefit Quebec and Canada's economy in the medium and long term. For the immediate future, like all governments, he was forced to maintain a delicate balance between the need to sustain the economic growth and his desire to fight the deficit. Some will say this is not enough, but as Quebec Minister of Finance, I am satisfied with these measures", concluded Mr. Levesque.
Following the tabling of the budget some said that the proposed measures were not sufficient. I believe that we have to be realistic. On the one hand it is interesting to note that our message finally got through and that the
public is now aware of the negative impact of a large debt. Now that the citizens of our country are convinced like us of the importance of our efforts, this will certainly help us keep going in the same direction.
For a long time we had the impression of preaching in the desert. However, our tenacity and the firm belief that we were right succeeded in making Canadians more responsible and understand that the debt is not only the government's problem but also their problem as taxpayers. Canadians now realize that the services which they have been enjoying are not free and that it is they who in the end must foot the bill one way or another.
This new awareness explains why some now say that we are not going far enough. To those people I say that based on the realism which has always guided our government, the implementation of drastic measures at this point would have adversely affected economic recovery and consequently federal revenue. As the minister of finance in Quebec said, and I quote: "Every time there are cuts, it affects the economy and this does not help government revenue".
As a responsible government we must take realistic measures which will not affect recovery and especially job creation because this is the way, and it is the only way, that we will be able to reach our goals, namely the reduction of the deficit and the growth of our economy in co-operation with all our partners.
I am therefore very pleased to see that the Quebec government is willing to co-operate with us to harmonize its fiscal policies, and I do hope that all the other provincial governments will follow suit. It is not through confrontation but rather through dialogue that we can make great things happen, and this is very true in the case of the economy.
This budget is tabled at a time when the public has never been so concerned with the expenditures and borrowings of our various governments. This concern is justified. Canadians know that they cannot indefinitely let the debit balance of their credit cards increase and then borrow just to pay interest. They saw what happens when a government behaves as though it was not subjected to the same basic rules of common sense.
What happens then is that taxpayers have to pay more and more for fewer and fewer government services because the interest takes an increasing portion of each dollar in tax revenue. Increasingly heavier taxes slow
April 28, 1993

down the economy, which in turn impedes job creation. Owners pay higher mortgage rates because government borrowings result in higher interest rates on loans. And higher interest rates have a deterring effect on investors and consumers, which also contributes to slowing down growth and job creation.
Finally, in order to maintain a standard of living which no longer matches our revenue, we rely more and more on foreign lenders. Our country becomes less and less in control of its economy, and an increasing part of our revenue must be used to pay interest to those foreign lenders.
Canadians want to remain in control of their future. They want their government to have the means to maintain essential social services as well as some fiscal flexibility when faced with new priorities.
To reduce borrowing and taxes, increase employment, and expand possibilities; those are the goals of Canadians. It is in this direction that our government has been going since 1984 and we will stay the course. More jobs, a strong and growing economy, and more choices.
First and foremost, we must maintain, and we will maintain, our strict and responsible policy regarding expenditure control.
Since 1984-85 we have made very real progress in an uncertain, changing international climate. We have reduced the annual growth in federal program spending from 13.8 per cent to 4.1 per cent. We have cut the federal deficit as a proportion of national revenue from
8.7	per cent to 5.1 per cent. Thanks to tight spending control, we have changed an operating deficit into an operating surplus, which means that the government is now spending less on its programs and services than it collects in revenue, and this has been the case for six years.
In the past few years a persistent painful economic slowdown throughout the world has forced governments, businesses and households, both in Canada and abroad, to change their future plans. This has accelerated the fundamental restructuring of our economy in the face of global economic change.
The Budget
To help Canadians deal with the economic slowdown and adjust to world competition, we took resolute measures in the 1992 budget and last December's economic statement. We reduced the income tax on individuals. We improved and restructured the child benefit plan so as to help low and middle income families. This will put $1.7 billion in the economy this year alone. We established the home buyers' Plan to help Canadians buy or build a house with funds in their RRSP.
As I have repeated so often, as responsible individuals we must not leave our children and grandchildren with a poisoned heritage. We have a responsibility to build a strong and prosperous society in which future generations can develop and fulfil themselves when it is their turn to take over.
I will conclude by saying that despite the energetic spending control measures taken by our government since 1984, Canada is still faced with the serious problems of rising public debt and the very high costs of servicing it. If we do not control the deficit we will suffer the consequences. The economy will be weaker, jobs will be even more scarce and it will not be possible to maintain the programs to which we are attached.
Our government has taken difficult but necessary measures. It has the situation under control. It has a concrete way to achieve its objective and, as we see light at the end of the tunnel, I trust that everyone will co-operate to help us so that together we can manage in a reasonable time to reduce and, why not, eliminate this weight that each of us is dragging, namely the deficit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could not let the member go without making a couple of short comments.
The way this government has mastered the art of propaganda is unbelievable. This is a government that was elected nine years ago stating that it was going to be the champion of focusing on deficit and debt reduction. Yet here we are nine years later with a debt that has at least doubled in the last nine years.
What is amazing about these speeches this afternoon, and I listened to the Minister of Employment and Immigration as well, is that things are being said like no tax increases, no increases to the deficit and no cuts to

April 28, 1993
The Budget
the provinces. The member just said that the government has reduced taxes to individuals. Does this government think that Canadians are stupid?
We have had 33 personal tax increases. Does the government think that Canadians have forgotten about the GST? What does it think when it says no cuts to the provinces? It cut out program spending which helps create jobs and now the welfare payments in this country are ballooning in every province because there are no capital works projects or special recovery projects for people to work at.
The government cut here but there is a welfare expense to the province and then it wonders why there is a provincial debt. This government has systematically dismantled the national government in the last nine years. It stands up all day long and throws out this con job, this propaganda, that all of a sudden it is focused on deficit and debt.
I cannot believe for a second that the member really believes her own speech. If she were to compare what she just said to what the Ministers of Finance have been saying on behalf of this government over the last nine years she will see, and I think Canadians realize, that there is absolutely no consistency and no trust left in this . Conservative government from the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will tell my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood that I am quite confident this government will be re-elected. When people are in the voting booth and compare how the Liberals ran the country when they were in office and the way we have done, how we had the courage to take tough measures, I am not worried, people will know where to put their X on the ballot.
By way of explanation I will tell the hon. member that, when we came into power in 1984 we were left with a poisoned legacy. If we had run things the same way as the Liberals did in the previous 15 years the national debt would now be $800 billion to $900 billion. Because we reduced program spending and administered judiciously we were able to limit the debt growth to $450 billion.
I want to tell the hon. member that we made every possible effort. I would therefore like to give him a few small points of comparison with the former Liberal government and show him how we governed, despite all the constraints we had, like a growing Canadian population and a whole lot of other things.
First, let us compare the two recessions. In the 1980-81 recession the deficit was $14.7 billion. In 1984-85 it was $38.5 billion. It more than doubled in that period; it grew 160 per cent. In 1989-90 the deficit was $29 billion and in 1992-93 it was $35.5 billion. This is an increase of less than one-fifth 20 per cent.
Now let us compare the deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product. In 1984-85 it was 8.7 per cent of GDP. In 1993-94 the deficit will only be 4.5 per cent of GDP, a reduction of 50 per cent. If we compare the growth in spending, the average under 15 years of Liberal rule was 13.8 per cent a year. Since 1984-85 it has averaged 3.6 per cent. Comparing Canada with the United States, in 1992-93 Canada's deficit was 5 per cent of GDP compared to 5.1 per cent in the United States. It is expected that in 1997-98 Canada will have a surplus equivalent to 0.1 per cent of GDP, while the United States will still have a deficit of 2.5 per cent of its GDP. Does the member want me to continue?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see you in the chair although I am sorry to afflict you with what I am going to have to say. You never know, I might convert you.
I have been through a number of these budget debates since 1968. I have listened to Conservatives kicking the heck out of Liberals about what they were doing in their budgets. Boy, the whole country was going to grind to a halt over what they were doing, to hear them tell it. They were very specific.
When they got through with that, I will be darned if they did not get elected. The next thing we know the Liberals are in opposition and the Conservatives are in the government.
As one might expect, the Liberals asked the Conservatives exactly the same questions.
April 28, 1993

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Conservatives gave them the same answers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. They were doing exactly the same things.
I rushed over from the committee meeting and got some notes which I am not going to use. While I was in my office I had the TV on. There was a member from the government side talking about food banks. If there is anything a Tory should never talk about, it is a food bank.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He was complaining about how the Liberals caused them. They both caused them. As a result of the economic policies of consecutive Liberal and Tory governments we have been afflicted with food banks. The member who spoke from the government side said they are being closed down. I would sure like her to find me one. If she can, it will only be closed because it could not get enough funds and supplies to keep it open. It would be for no other reason.
Government cabinet ministers have talked about
200,000	new jobs created but I still do not know where they are. A whole bunch of my constituents have not been able to find them and it is not as bad in my city as it is in the cities of both of my colleagues here.
Let us go into this business of deficits and debts. Any government of any political stripe that becomes so hypnotized, terrorized and mesmerized by the size of the current deficit and the accumulated debt becomes immobilized.
If we learned nothing else from the dirty thirties it was that it was the time one spent money one did not have. The current taxpayers and their successors, their children and grandchildren, would have to pay it off.
For a fundamental civilized Christian reason we do not treat people that way in tough times. We just do not do it. Much fuss has been made about the $450 million or $480 billion of the current debt of Canada and the current deficit of $35.5 billion that will get added on to the national debt.
What else is new? I want to say something. I am a child of the dirty thirties. Successive Conservative and Liberal governments in my poor begotten province did not pay their bills. They lost the store. In fact, they bankrupted the whole province.
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They did not pay their bills that had accumulated from previous years. They should have borrowed some more money, put people to work and then they could have paid their bills.
I am just an ordinary prairie country boy. I am not a fancy economist or financier but it just seems to me that it makes common sense.
Some of the national debt goes back to 1930 because governments in those years could not make their payments and they piled up. They would put out another bond issue to pay off the previous one. If we took that and all the debt that was accumulated during the war at the end of 1945, added up the total national debt and translated in 1993 dollars it would be just as high or higher than it is now. What else is new? We have been through this before. We have to rely on the people, put them to work and the national government has to provide the leadership.
The hon. member for Vegreville, the Minister of Finance, is a good friend and an easy fellow to like. He and I are colleagues from the class of '68. He looks a heck of a lot younger than I do and I am not sure if he is. I never thought I would live to see the day when my hon. friend from Vegreville, the Minister of Finance, would sound like R. B. Bennett and Mackenzie King of 1935 or 1938. The government has not learned anything in 60 or 70 years, in fact it has never learned anything from experience. It does not have to believe me. It does not have to listen to the NDP. It does not have to listen to those terrible socialists.
In country after country in Europe it was the socialists who bailed them out of their economic and financial mess. In 1944, when members of the old CCF-bless their hearts-formed the government led by Tommy Douglas the accumulated debt went back to 1930. In fact two issues of bonds were defaulted upon as the Tory and Liberal governments could not make the payments and the federal government had to step in and pick them up. There were those debts from the dirty thirties plus what happened in the Second World War. Most of the taxation ability went to the federal authority for the war effort which nobody complained about and the provinces starved.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
From 1930 to 1945 the deficit of the province of Saskatchewan was as big as it is today. Today thanks to the beautiful blessings of one Grant Devine, the late unlamented premier of Saskatchewan, our debt is now bigger than it was then. When Liberals and Tories talk to me about running governments according to sound business practice, the only kind of business they are in is misleading the people of this country and ruining the economy of this country.
I will not be here much longer. This is my last term but I have listened to the same damn thing every bloody year since 1968. I do not ask anybody to believe me, listen to me, pay attention or do anything about anything I say. I ask them to look at what has happened while they were here. If we do not learn from history and from our own actions we are condemned to repeat them and the government is repeating these in spades.
This budget does nothing about the deficit or debt. Why? Because in the traditional old-line party practice in tough times everybody has to be careful and cut back.
I look at the financial pages. I inherited some shares in a company that was supposed to be going great guns. It is in a resource industry. I think they should call it "the dry hole drilling company". It has gone from $10 a share down to I think 13 cents now.
That is what has occurred under private enterprise governments. Their friends who have those shares made a bundle. They bought them at ten bucks. I refuse to buy stocks. I inherited the ones I have, a whole 100 shares. I have fun looking at the financial pages. I have begun to look at other issues of bonds and stocks.
There is the whole issue of privatizing. It is terrible for the government to own anything. It is going to privatize Air Canada for example. It conned 4,000 employees, even though I told them not to, into buying shares at ten bucks a share. It told them of the glories of free enterprise, profits, dividends, ad nauseam. You will be lucky, Mr. Speaker, to get three bucks for those shares. If you can get three bucks for them and if anybody in this place has them get rid of them quick.
We have been in the hands of incompetents. When they talk about governing according to sound business
practices I would not let them manage my chicken coop if I had one. I am not just criticizing the government. I say the same thing about the Liberals. They were masters at it.
When the Liberals got excited about the deficit and the debt they made some cutbacks. Not as many as we have today but for those days there were quite a few. You should have heard those stories. They were up screaming their heads off about those cutbacks. They raised hell. They moved want of confidence motions. The cuts were as welcome as a skunk at a garden party. That is how they acted.
Then the Tories defeated the Liberals, as if that was a big deal. I will be darned. The next thing I know the Liberals are getting up raising heck about the Tory cutbacks. Thlk about pots calling kettles black. That is a little much. They sure did not fool us fellows down at this end of the Chamber. I do not think they fooled many people in the country. When I go to Gopher Gulch and Grasshopper Flats and when my colleagues go back home to their people or when they travel around this country, we find it is not being swallowed. It is not being believed.
We have moved a subamendment. It is not only to try to defeat the government. That is a minor detail. That is going to happen anyway, if not this year then next year, whenever. It is not long for this world. We moved on a basis of some kind of principle and policy. We are having a little difficulty with the Tories enunciating policy because they are victimized with the present government, especially Tory candidates for the leadership. They are a little bit hard put to announce policies. However I do not hear any nuts and bolts policies from the Liberals. I have listened to them for, God knows, 45 years, my membership in the NDP. In fact, the Liberals forced me into joining the NDP. They forced me. After I got out of the Armed Forces after the Second World War, I said: "My God, it's the only place for me to go". They drove me out, and they still drive me out.
There is nothing so obnoxious as a reformed sinner. If the hon. gentleman had just told me to come back, I would ask come back to what? He did not mind telling me to come back to what. If it is different from what we have got now I will be glad to listen to him.
April 28, 1993

It was no great move philosophically for somebody to move from the Tories to the Liberal Party, and vice versa. In the years I have been here I have seen a whole bunch of them do that. They can do it without even blushing. They do not even know how to do it the right way. The first thing you do is tell your leader, your caucus and then your own membership. Then you resign your seat and run for re-election with whatever new party you have chosen. That is called honour in politics. You wonder why Joe Citizen says "those damned politicians". That is one of the reasons. You have got the ethics of a tomcat that just came out of a back alley.
If I ever had to part company with the NDP-I do not think it will happen, I hope it never will-I would let the party know ahead of time at the national, provincial and federal levels. I would have the courtesy to tell it and then I would quit and get out of the way. Let it do what it wants to do because it would not listen to me before. That should apply to every member of any party.
Some people say we need a two party system. If it were a choice between the Grits and the Tories that would only be a one party system. The communists could take lessons. There is no fundamental basic philosophical difference between them. One wants to do "open for business, free enterprise, marketplace" quicker than the other.
Somebody should tell me what the difference is. When I said that those governments of any political party are hypnotized, I meant it. When they become so hypnotized, so mesmerized and so terrorized that they become immobilized then they have lost sight of the fact of why they are there, what they are there for and what they are there to do.
When the good times come is when to put money in the bank through taxes and whatnot. "Save for the rainy days", my mother always said. When it is bad times you share with all your fellow Canadians what it costs in order to have all of them live decently, in a decent home, with enough money for food and full opportunity for their children. We share that. If we are not going to share it we become the old 19th century jungle.
This budget puts us and keeps us in the jungle. I would be glad to pay an extra 1 per cent or 2 per cent or
The Budget
whatever on my income tax if I knew it would go toward that purpose. Nobody objects to the amount of taxes they pay if they know what they are going for and who they are going to benefit.
Today at a committee meeting there were a couple of individuals who make more than $250,000 a year. The poor fellows. When I see them I see corporations that make a profit. Even after their write-offs they do not pay any taxes. Now that is not totally unjustified and unfair. It was not just done by this government. The Liberals were saddled with it. In fact I think they started it.

speechtext:
It goes back farther than that. They started giving those kind of benefits to corporations in the late 1930s and the early 1940s.
We are not going to be a party to this by either party. For all I know the Liberals are going to vote for our subamendment. I hope they do not because then I will worry about what we are doing wrong.
