subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The reason I am participating in this debate is to talk about some of the good things in this budget, some of the things that have probably been mentioned by some of my colleagues and some of the things that have been opposed by some of those on the other side of the House. I would like to very briefly run through what I think are some of the highlights of the budget.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
One of the first highlights in my opinion is the fact that there is no tax increase. I believe this is our third budget in which we have been able to do so. I have been here for five budgets. I feel quite comfortable in saying that we did not raise taxes in this budget, we did not introduce any new taxes in this budget and this is the third year we have managed to do that. In fact last year we reduced taxes in a number of areas. I wish we could have done that again this year.
For those who might say there were no tax changes simply because it is an election year, I can only refer back to last year and the year before and point out there were no tax changes in those years either.
Basically there are no tax increases in this because we on this side of the House understand what our constituents are saying and that is no tax increases. I am happy to say there are none.
There is another very positive aspect about this budget. There is no real growth in spending. I sent out a questionnaire to my constituents called "You be the finance minister". I asked them to tell how they would spend money if they were the finance minister.
Consistently the responses that came back to me were to freeze spending. In some cases they would have a little more in one area, offset by a saving in another, so that the bottom line remained the same. I am happy to report that this budget does exactly that. It freezes spending, the total amount, at what it was last year so there is no real growth in spending. Personally I think that is a very positive situation.
It goes a little further than that though as far as my view on this budget and why it is positive. There are some real important changes in this budget. There is one change that is in here that I might point out. If some member would like to ask me a question in a few moments about the helicopter contract, I would be happy to respond as to why I think it is such a good idea that this budget does not touch the helicopter contract.
Over and above that there are things it does touch and I would like to really emphasize those, such as the need for provincial co-operation. The deficit and debt of the Government of Canada are not just a problem of the federal government, but a problem that all the provincial governments have as well. What we have done with this budget is to say look let us bring everybody together,
discuss the areas where we have a problem and see if we can arrive at some common solution between us. I think that is very positive.
There have been some cuts unfortunately but some of the cuts I do not have a problem supporting. For example the ERDA agreements. We hear the business community all the time talking about cutting grants to business. Lo and behold what did we do? We cancelled, we stopped funding the forestry economic agreements, the mining economic agreements. These are agreements which put taxpayer funds into private enterprise. We have cut them. It is interesting now that the business community affected by those cuts is complaining but that is the way life goes. Everybody expects you to cut, just not in their area.
More important, we have also signalled to all the provinces affected with the various economic development agreements that when their particular agreement comes up-there is a list of 10 or 12 of them-for renewal those in fact will be looked at and discussed and simply not automatically renewed. I think that is very positive.
We have talked about Public Service reform. I note Bob Rae in Ontario is talking about how he is going to cut 10,000 employees out of 900,000. He says Tories in Ottawa do not know how to do it. Well, 10,000 out of
900,000	versus our proposal for 16,500 out of 250,000. It seems to me Bob Rae has not got it quite right. To have the same equation he ought to be looking somehow at finding 50,000 or 60,000 jobs in the public service in Ontario that are not needed.
In fairness they may be needed and maybe Bob Rae cannot find more than 10,000 but if he is going to criticize our cuts he ought to look at the actual numbers to determine whether we are doing our share. I am happy to report that we are.
There are some other changes. There are the changes in the freight rate system we have in this country such as the Crow rate. I appreciate that does not affect my constituency. It is a very important benefit that we have established in this country for western Canadian grain farmers. We have said we are going to review that, we are going to see if there is some better way of helping grain farmers. That is a very positive thing to do.
Right now all we do is give that money to railroads. Maybe we ought to give it to the farmers to let them figure out if there is a better way of them bringing their
April 28, 1993

product to market than using the railroads, That is healthy and puts a little competition against the railroads. I bet there are some trucking companies that would be quite prepared to say that they can haul the grain for less than the railroads. That benefits everybody if one can create some real good competition.
What does the end result of this budget bring forward? It brings forward a very important aspect of the debt and the deficit in this country. Deficits are of course a function of one's ability to pay. Our ability to pay has been improving. When we were elected the deficit as a percentage of the gross domestic product was over 8 per cent. This budget foresees that at the end of the next period of fiscal responsibility, which is a five-year phase, we expect that to be down to less than 1 per cent. That is a very positive step toward getting rid of the deficit that we have in front of us. We can better make the payments.
What is the opposition's alternative to that 1 per cent target? Its alternative is that we should have a 3 per cent target. That is certainly better than it is today. Today we are approaching 4 per cent. They think it ought to be 3 per cent. I commend them for that but why do we stop at 3 per cent? Why in this country should we be happy with a deficit of $25 billion or $20 billion a year? It was that mentality of the 1970s that got us into the 1980s and into the 1990s with this huge debt we have. There is this idea that it is okay to have 3 per cent of the income as a deficit. That is unacceptable.
I see in this budget that the Minister of Finance is very clearly saying that as we go out for the five-year period we are not only going to be below 4 per cent, the 3 per cent Liberal target and the 2 per cent target, we are going to have it down to less than 1 per cent.
What do all of those things do to the Canadian economy? We have had some discussion in this House about the forecasts that exist by various monitoring agencies about growth in Canada. I am happy to see that the International Monetary Fund is forecasting a growth in Canada of 4.4 per cent next year, which is the highest rate of growth of the seven major countries that they compared us to: United Kingdom, Italy, France, Germany, Japan and the U.S. None of them have a 4.4 per cent
The Budget
growth. We are number one next year in the forecast and of course for 1993 we will continue to be number one.
There are two other areas that I would very briefly like to touch on which emanate from last year's budget and that in a sense were responded to in this budget. Last year the finance committee did a review of the issue of quarterly instalments that people would have to pay if they owed income tax of $1,000 a year or less.
We recommended that level be raised. Now Canadians who owe $2,000 a year or less in income tax do not have to file quarterly instalments. That is a very direct recommendation that went to the Minister of Finance from the finance committee and, lo and behold, he delivered. It is very positive and very good for a lot of Canadians whether they are seniors or low income Canadians. In Canada it affects an awful lot of people very positively.
The second thing he dealt with was regulatory reform. In last year's budget the Minister of Finance asked the finance committee to review the process of regulatory reform in this country because it impacts on Canadian business and ultimately in the cost of everything Canadians buy in this country.
The finance committee set up a subcommittee that I chaired. I am happy to say that we issued a report back in September and filed it through to the House. The President of the Treasury Board today responded to this as a direct result of the previous budget. People will find that the Government of Canada has again listened to the problems and concerns of Canadians and the impact that they can have on business. Today we have a very positive response about changes they can make to the regulatory process.
Those are some of things that have caused me to be very positive about this budget. There are really many others. The ultimate feeling I have on this budget is to emphasize that the Government of Canada said no to spending increases, no to tax increases and yes to fiscal responsibility.
That is what I believe in and that is why I am here. I am glad to be able to support this budget because of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much impressed with the presentation of the hon. member. We were listening carefully to those very good factual comments he was making. He mentioned that he does

April 28, 1993
The Budget
favour the purchase of helicopters. This has been very controversial in Canada. Personally I also agree with it. Could he perhaps enlighten us further as to some of these very valid reasons why the Canadian government should proceed with the helicopter purchase?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that question. Right through my years of political involvement and in advance of that, I have always had the opinion that Canadian forces should have some of the most modern technology available. Part of the reason I had that opinion was because there were spin-off benefits to Canadians by having them supply modem technology.
I would just like to share a letter I received from one of my constituents in a business in Whitby called Andrew Canada Inc. It employs 154 people and has been located in the town of Whitby since 1953. It provides, among other things, communications technology to the helicopter program. It says, to be very blunt:
We are currently negotiating a contract to design, develop and manufacture airborne radar antennas for the helicopters. Through technology transfer agreements related to the program we will acquire new, specialized skills and know-how which will not only enable us to fulfil the helicopter contract, but will also allow us to become recognized participants in the future airborne antenna market world-wide. The benefits of the program to us are potentially long term in excess of 15 years.
I should point out that there is a further benefit because I know that that is great for my riding. The letter
goes on to say:
Technology benefits will also flow down to our intended subcontractor in the maritimes, who will acquire new techniques for the fabrication of antenna reflectors.
I am happy to see that my concept of government buying technologically advanced pieces of equipment has the benefit of first giving our forces the proper modem equipment they should have, but secondly and more importantly, providing spin-off benefits. Very clearly here is a case in point where there will be spin-off benefits that will enable Canadian companies to be competitive world-wide with technologies.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. The hon. member for Cambridge. They have split their time, just for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to participate in this year's budget debate.
I believe that the budget presented a couple of evenings ago is a credible fiscal plan with very realistic objectives. I think in recognition of the need to further enhance Canada's competitive position and the economic recovery, as my colleague mentioned just a few moments ago, the budget included no new taxes.
Another benefit I thought in the budget was that the fiscal plan features tight control over program spending with the growth held to the rate of inflation. In other words there is no growth at all in real terms.
My colleague, the member for Ontario mentions the finance committee. Two years ago our committee work included the development of the Spending Control Act. That resulted in a 3 per cent cap on the growth of program spending. This meant if expenditures on a program rose above the projection that it would have to be offset by reductions elsewhere.
The Spending Control Act did not allow increased borrowing or increased taxes to fund spending that was higher than planned. That was two years ago with a 3 per cent cap.
Of course we all know that as a result of this government's policies inflation now is below 2 per cent. I thought it was probably a good idea that maybe we should take a look at lowering this cap. That was my main recommendation to the Minister of Finance in the discussions leading up to the preparation of the budget. I am happy to say that he did listen.
I believe the new target that will be established will be
1.7	per cent. If we were to take a comparable figure from the U.S.A., it is 3.3 per cent. By putting controls and more caps on spending this will result in a savings of almost $3 billion by 1995.
People will ask whether this is a realistic target. I believe it is. The proposed spending control limit last year was $100.1 billion for the 1992-93 fiscal year. For that fiscal year the Minister of Finance presented main estimates of $99.1 billion. As such the 1993 budget presents a fiscally responsible plan that will deal with the federal deficit.
April 28, 1993

As acknowledged by the Minister of Finance there is only one taxpayer to foot the bills. The fiscal problem is a national problem that must be addressed by all levels of government working together.
Passing the federal fiscal problems on to the provinces would not have been productive especially from a taxpayer's point of view. Therefore the 1993 budget could have cut deeper and more quickly but this inevitably would have required substantial cuts in the major transfers to provinces.
However, in recognition of the fiscal difficulties that provinces are confronting the federal government chose to exempt transfers to provinces from further restraint. Instead of cutting transfers to provinces the budget laid out a process that will lead to a combined federal-provincial approach to our national debt problem.
Why has the Minister of Finance in recognition of Canada's collective fiscal problem asked his provincial counterparts to attend this special meeting? The purpose is to begin working with the federal government on a co-operative approach to developing practical solutions to the national debt problem.
I want to put a few facts on the record. In 1984-85 the federal deficit was $38.5 billion. In this year's budget it is $35 billion. In essence it stayed the same in dollar terms. The total deficit of all the provinces in 1984 was just slightly over $8 billion. Today the deficit of all provinces is $24 billion, which is a 300 per cent increase.
The message is that the provincial administrations now show the same symptoms that plagued the federal Liberals in the early 1980s: a combination of large deficits, growing debts and rising debt charges that mutually fuel each other.
Let us look at some of the pressures that were on governments to spend prior to today. We know for example that between 1975 and 1990 the combined health, social services and education sectors represented a large and growing source of spending pressure.
Relative to total program spending between 1975 and 1990 these health, social services and education costs rose by almost 5 percentage points as a percentage of gross domestic product.
The Budget
What other factors have resulted in an increase in the GDP share of spending? First, we all know and recognize the growth in interest charges on the public debt. A second one is the growth in health care spending primarily reflected in the growing per capita demand for medical services.
When we talk about health care spending, what are some of the factors that are causing health care spending to increase? First, we have the aging of the Canadian population. We are seeing new medical technologies which result in new treatments. We are also seeing the growth in the number of services per physician within a system that pays physicians on a fee for service basis.
That is the past and we all recognize those pressures on spending. What about the future? Where are we going to see the future pressures on spending? One will be because of changes in demands for existing programs. For example, the aging of the population will continue to increase and as a proportion of the population the demand for medical care and age care facilities will clearly increase.
At the same time there will be a drop in the age of university students that will result in lower university enrolment. We are seeing the same pressures, because of the economic restructuring, on unemployment insurance, in the Canada Assistance Plan and in labour market training.
People want to see more money spent on environment and justice issues. We have some things that are going to lower the cost to government such as falling interest rates, falling inflation and certainly the increased public concern on the over-all level of taxation.
What I want to do is quickly summarize. The spending pressures I have mentioned on health care, education, employee retraining, environment and justice are all issues that are a joint responsibility between the provinces and Ottawa. In many cases Ottawa is just a silent financial partner. It makes sense to me that if we are going to deal with these spending pressures, does Ottawa do it unilaterally? Does the finance minister just say that this is the way it is going to be and download the problems on to the provinces? Or do they want to work together?

April 28, 1993
The Budget
I congratulate the finance minister who has demonstrated the desire to give co-operative federalism a chance to work and an opportunity so that all governments at all levels can move in the same direction in reducing the debt and encouraging economic growth.
I trust that in that forum the moral suasion of the taxpayers will encourage the federal and provincial finance ministers to succeed together.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one really has to wonder why the finance minister brought in his spring 1993 budget. It is completely lifeless. It has no imagination, no ideas, no strategy to address our pressing economic problems and no hope for the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians.
It shows beyond all doubt that this government has run out of gas. It is old and tired. The only thing left is for this government to be put away into the history books. I am confident Canadian voters will do just that in the coming election.
This budget must be particularly galling to the few remaining supporters of federal Conservatives who believe the government was serious about attacking the deficit. The budget does nothing about deficit reduction. In fact it forecasts an increase of over $1 billion in the deficit.
To many of us, however, that comes as no surprise. This government has talked big about deficit reduction, almost from the first day it took office in 1984. Consider the fact that the deficit is $8 billion over its 1992 projection, a projection given by the finance minister. Right now it stands well over $30 billion. In the meantime our debt under almost nine years of Tory rule has shot up well over 100 per cent, from about $169 billion to almost $460 billion.
This government has howled long and hard about the deficit it inherited. That may well have been fair at the time it took office, but the government cannot avoid its responsibilities. It has had nine long years to deal with our deficit and debt problems and in that regard it has failed miserably. Blaming politicians from another time just does not wash.
The 1993 budget does absolutely nothing to address the severe problems of unemployment. There are at
least 1.5 million Canadians out of work and I suspect the real figure is well above that. There is no hope for the unemployed in this budget. There are no attempts at job creation, no strategy to get people back to work. Let us face it. Until we dramatically reduce unemployment there is no hope of returning to prosperity and attacking the deficit in both absolute terms and as a percentage of the gross domestic product.
Over and above the pain they inflict on workers and their families the huge unemployment figures are damaging to the economy. It is estimated the cost of one million unemployed Canadians is somewhere between $20 billion and $25 billion annually. A big chunk of that is the payout through unemployment insurance, $19 billion a year right now. That is a huge cost to our economy. Think what we could do with $19 billion if the unemployed were working. I should say here that the $19 billion does not include welfare payments.
Moreover, if we create jobs for the unemployed they in turn will regain their rightful status as productive citizens. They will pay taxes on their earnings. That is how the government wall be able to reduce, if not totally eliminate the deficit.
Economic growth and creating jobs are the essential tools in attacking the deficit. Another tool is controlling government spending and eliminating waste is part of that. This government believes only that cuts in government services promise a return to prosperity. That is not true. Without economic growth, without creating jobs, this economy is not going anywhere. It can talk all it wants about increased productivity but if we do not get economic growth and we do not get more jobs, the economy is not going anywhere.
Canada needs a new vision. Canada needs new fiscal management. The old Tory crowd does not have it. They are over their heads. At a time like this my advice to the government is quite simple: Stand aside and let someone with ideas and vision take over.
We have a vision. We have proposed, for example, an infrastructure program to pump some life in the short term back into the economy. A renewed physical infrastructure is one of the building blocks of a new prosperity. We have proposed a national apprenticeship program. This would involve the co-operation of senior govern-
April 28, 1993

ments, the private sector, labour and educational institutions.
The private sector needs trained young workers. Many students grow disillusioned with the traditional school system. I should point out that Germany graduates about
600,000	apprentices a year while we graduate only 24,000. An apprenticeship program would be a challenging alternative for many of these students. It would help them make the transition from school into the work force.
We also propose a Canada youth service. This program would enable young people to give service to their country and develop essential skills and work habits in the process.
We would build a value added economy. That is the way of the future. We are far too prone in Canada to market raw materials. When we ship raw materials out of the country for processing, we are shipping jobs out of Canada. That is why we assign so much importance to value added activity.
We would revitalize the small business sector. While the government has been cosying up to big international business, small business has been neglected. When the government was killing the economy with high interest rates and the high dollar, the pleas of small business were ignored. Ask small businesses about their problems in getting financial assistance from banks or other financial institutions. We are committed to addressing that problem.
We are also committed to a global trade strategy. I emphasize it is a global trade strategy. Beyond our difficulties with the free trade agreement, our trading interests transcend the United States. We must look for trade growth in Latin America and the Pacific Rim.
Another move we Liberals would make, and this perhaps is the most important of all, is that we would forge new partnerships with all stakeholders in Canada. That includes the provinces, the private sector, labour, the municipalities and volunteer agencies. We have thought long and hard about this new approach to our problems because the Tory approach has been a disaster.
Leaving it to the big boys does not work. Trickle down does not work. It did not work in Britain. It did not work in the United States, where trickle down took that country from the greatest creditor country to the great-
The Budget
est debtor nation. That took only eight years under that dreadful actor from Hollywood.
Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the finance minister's budget is its central message and that message is this: Tory economics work, everything is okay and the government is not changing a thing, it is staying the course. It is that message that tells us just how out of touch this government is.
I want to remind everyone that there are at least 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Almost 400,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost, lost forever. There have been over 200,000 business and personal bankruptcies since 1989 and about one million Canadians depend on food banks every year. Despite the havoc wrought by Tory policies the finance minister pays no attention to them. If he had admitted to even some self-doubt perhaps his budget would have received more understanding.
Marshall Cohen, the chief executive officer of the Molson companies, recently questioned the standard faith of neo-conservative economics. That faith says that the current economic restructuring will pay off, that ultimately for every job eliminated two will be created. Mr. Cohen says it is time to question that faith and it is time to think that Canada is not heading for a jobless recovery but a jobless economy.
I think Mr. Cohen is in touch with reality. This government's finance minister is not. His mind is elsewhere. There is no indication that he will ever come to his senses. There is only one remedy for this. All Canadians know what that remedy is and I think they are more than eager to apply it at the next election.
I want to finish by saying that the budget cuts about $90 million from regional development in the current fiscal year and another $100 million in 1995. To me that is madness. Regional development has been a unique Canadian way to develop the economy from coast to coast. It has been of particular help to the have-less regions. I come from a have-less region.
In Winnipeg we have called for a new core area agreement. This budget is not going to give us that. We have called for a new cultural industries agreement, something like the one we had a few years ago, one that created a lot of jobs and provided a lot of spin-offs in the economy. It looks like we are not going to get it. This budget does absolutely nothing for the port of Churchill,

April 28, 1993
The Budget
a port that must be preserved and if preserved would be a great help to prairie farmers.
I will conclude by adding one comment to a remark made by the member for Ontario. He boasted about this budget taking 300,000 Canadians off the list who until now have paid quarterly income tax instalments. He is right that far. What he neglected to say is that while the government is proposing to take 300,000 people off that list, the government has added 500,000 new names to the list of those who have to pay quarterly tax instalments. I wanted to mention that in order that his remarks are put in their proper context.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to put a few comments on the record about employment.
The manufacturing sector in Ontario has begun to see the recovery. Since October manufacturing employment has risen by 2.5 per cent or 42,000 jobs in Ontario. Since August 1992 in Canada full-time employment has increased 200,000. So far this year full-time employment has increased 66,000 across Canada. At this pace that would represent a 260,000 job increase. I wanted to put those comments on the record.
I would also like to put this comment on the record. This comes from Conestoga College. It is a release indicating its graduates are doing well in securing employment. It says: "The 1991-92 graduates of Conestoga College did well in locating and securing employment within six months of completing their program of study. Of the 838 graduates available for employment, 694 almost 700, or 83 per cent were successful. In spite of the economic uncertainty employers continue to demonstrate their confidence in our program by hiring Conestoga College graduates. Eighty-two per cent of our graduates found employment, 62 per cent of them directly related to the their programs".
This is excellent news in these times of high unemployment. Conestoga College in Kitchener is doing an excellent job in producing graduates. I wonder if the hon. member wants to congratulate the students in their success, but also all those companies that are starting to grow, making employment for these graduating students.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always prepared to offer my congratulations to anyone who is able to
prosper in this country, to do well despite Tory economic policies and that is what is happening. A lot of people out there are showing plenty of resourcefulness and industry despite the disastrous policies of the government.
Let me just say that this member and all other members on that side of the House can crow about certain success stories. That is fine in itself, but we are not going to have true prosperity and success in turning the economy around until we get people back to work. It is a Pyrrhic victory. That is what it is.
The member for Cambridge mentions those figures. They are happy figures. I am happy for them, but we have to address unemployment. Until we get the unemployment figures down we will not get the deficit down, we will not get the debt down, and we really will not have a return of prosperity. That is where the government is wrong. It does not seem to understand that until it attacks the unemployment problem this economy is never going to go anywhere.
Having increased productivity and increased trade figures is only a partial answer. It does not answer the misery people are feeling out there. There is a lot of despair because they do not have jobs and they lack confidence in the future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget is nothing more than a stale leftover from last December's failed economic statement, twice warmed over and reheated. In fact in the dying days of this Conservative government I cannot help but think of this budget as one of the first signs of rigor mortis setting in.
There is absolutely nothing in this budget that will get the economy moving again and will put Canadians back to work. Canada's 11 per cent unemployment is the highest of any G-7 country. There are 1.5 million Canadians still looking for work and suffering hardships in society that they should not be suffering in this day and age.
On page 21 of the budget the Minister of Finance says:
The medium-term projection underlying the fiscal plan is based
on the assumption that some excess capacity in labour and product
markets will remain through 1998.
April 28, 1993

The Budget
That is little hope for the unemployed. In plain English this has made it clear there will not be enough jobs for Canadians five years from now if this government stays in office.
Studies have confirmed that unemployed Canadians cost the federal government more than $20 billion a year each and every year this government remains in office. These unemployed people are not able to contribute to society, contribute to our economy and feed back through the system.
In 1991, 1.4 million Canadians were out of work and last year 1.5 million were out of work. If over the last two years half these people had been working, the government would have saved close to $40 billion. That is $10 billion more than this budget proposes to cut mostly four or five years from now.
Nor is there anything in this budget for Canadian youth who already face dismal summer job prospects. Youth unemployment is currently at 17.6 per cent. With this budget the government is now telling Canadians that it is going to solve all of its economic problems by assuming strong economic growth. Yet the government has no detailed economic plan to nurture innovation, training and infrastructure, the building blocks of a strong and prosperous economy.
However the government's own budget document states that projected growth "will not bring the economy to full capacity utilization for 1998". In other words, Canada is still in for five more years of recession-like conditions with economic activity at levels well below that of the 1980s.
There are no economic priorities in a $5.8 billion face-saving gesture for the Minister of National Defence. The budget keeps Canada's helicopter program intact, and meanwhile the Tories are stealing from the poor by postponing their January GST tax rebate.
The 1992-93 deficit is $8 billion higher than the Minister of Finance said it would be in the February 1992 budget and $1.1 billion more than he said it would be in his economic statement last December.
No wonder the dollar is dropping. No wonder there are questions about our credit rating. Not even Bay Street believes this government any more.
In 1989 the government forecasted a national debt of $440 billion in 1993-94. Now it is forecasting a debt of $491 billion. That is an increase of $51 billion over the last three years in its forecast. In fact the $35.5 billion deficit for 1992 is the highest deficit ever reported in the House of Commons. In 1984 when the government was first elected there was an accumulated debt of $168 billion, accumulated in the 117 years since Confederation.
However, after only nine years of this government's mismanagement, the debt ballooned to $458 billion. So much for fiscal management and the Conservative 1988 election slogan of "managing change".
This economy is not a gambling table. We need solid forecasting. We need solid projections. We need solid growth in this country. It cannot be achieved through the roll of the dice. So much for fiscal management.
The government claims the budget will deliver $30 billion in spending cuts and other measures. Only $3.8 billion is forecasted to be delivered in the upcoming fiscal year. Out of that $2.8 billion was already announced in December and $615 million is only a shift in the timing of the GST credit. Calling that a saving is like skipping December's mortgage payment and claiming in January that money has been saved.
The projections of the Minister of Finance confirm that the Conservative leadership candidates, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, were out to lunch when they promised to eliminate the deficit in four to five years respectively. Either that or the leading Tory leadership candidates are saying the Minister of Finance does not know what he is talking about.
More than the Minister of Finance do not know what they are talking about. The candidates do not know what they are talking about. Unless they come out with some creative new programs that will stimulate the economy it is going to get even worse.
There are no positive viewpoints. I should say that perhaps one of the things that might be close to being positive would be that there are no additional cuts to the federal-provincial transfer payments. Three hundred thousand Canadians, mostly senior citizens, will no longer have to pay income tax in quarterly instalments. I was pleased to see there were no further tax increases.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
However, after 38 consecutive tax increases by this government, this commitment is a case of too little too late.
Since 1984 revenues collected from persons have increased by 126 per cent while revenues collected from corporations have increased by only 1.8 per cent. This budget does not improve that. It offers yet another series of measures designed to save corporations $400 million over the next five years and no similar tax break for ordinary Canadians.
I do note in this budget document the government finally recognizes that since 1984 Canada has been buying more goods and services from other countries than we have been selling and thus we have had record current account deficits. I have spoken about this in the House before on at least three or four different occasions. Last spring Canada was running a record current account deficit of $29 billion. In 1984, before this government was elected, the current account deficit did not exist. There was a current account surplus of some $2.7 billion.
We have not had a single quarter, let alone a single year, in which we recorded current account surpluses since this government came to power. Arthur Donnor, a prominent economist, argues that each $20 billion worth of current account deficits equates to roughly 500,000 jobs lost. Now we know where the jobs went. It is the current account deficits.
The interest payments and the dividends going out of this country are draining our economy, a haemorrhage that must be stopped.
In terms of agriculture I was shocked to read the budget papers because I saw what was happening to the method of payment of the Crow. I am going to put on record a letter from Prairie Pools Inc. It says that the federal budget is a coercion. It is dated Monday, April 26, 1993. I quote:
The Federal Government's plan to cut an additional 10 per cent from its expenditures on western grain transportation assistance unless there is a change in the method of payment amounts to coercion of western grain and oilseed producers.
"It appears to us that since the government has not been able to get agreement from farmers to change the method of payment through consultation, it has decided to force the issue with spending cuts," said PPI Chairman Ken Edie.
The federal budget indicates that on top of the 10 per cent cut announced for 1993-94-another 5 per cent will be cut in 1995-96
and another 5 per cent will be cut in 1996-97. However, it also indicates that these cuts could be reallocated to support a change to a producer payment for the federal assistance.
The 10 per cent cuts announced in the December economic statement will remove $73 million from the prairie agriculture industry in each of the next two crop years. Tlie additional cuts announced in the budget today would take another $65 million out of the prairie farm economy. "These are cuts that farmers who are already suffering from depressed prices and rising input costs, can ill afford, " said Mr. Edie.
"Prairie farmers have always tried to work with governments to develop policy and programs in the best interests of the industry and the national economy," said Mr. Edie. "We believe that changes should be made through negotiation and agreement by all major stakeholders, not through strong arm methods".
To include such coercion in a budget that completely circumvents the consultation process is unacceptable to society. Where is the trust this country is built on?
We need something positive. We need to rekindle the spirit of pride that built this nation. We need to rekindle the spirit of positive programs, programs that those on this side of the House are prepared to deliver.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of my colleague from Lambton- Middlesex. He talked in terms of billions and I would like to put it in simpler terms.
Being from Ontario, when Bob Rae took office 12 cents of every tax dollar went to pay the debt. If he does not get his social contract with the 900,000 public servants in Ontario, by the end of two years 26 cents of every tax dollar will go toward the debt.
I mention this because people can understand it. Back in 1979 the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans stood in the House and proposed a budget of 18 cents a gallon, and the voters turfed him out because everyone could understand 18 cents.
In 1967 when the Liberals were in office, centennial year, 11 cents of every dollar went toward the debt. That left 89 cents for program spending. By 1983 as a result of Liberal fiscal management, 32 cents of every tax dollar went to pay interest on the debt and that left only 68 cents for programs plus what had to be borrowed.
Instead of talking in billions would the hon. member, my colleague from Ontario, please explain to me in simple terms how going from 11 cents of each tax dollar to 32 cents has not caused a hole, exactly the same hole
April 28, 1993

that Bob Rae is causing for the next government in Ontario?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the question. The member raised a very good issue. Over 24 years, from 1960 to 1983, the increased cost of servicing the debt amounted to 21 cents. Then in the Tory years that followed it ballooned to 43.2 cents.
I cannot speak on behalf of socialists in Ontario. I understand there is a difference of opinion between them and socialists here in Ottawa and I do not want to get into that today.
I point out that one thing that really concerns me is that a lot of those public debt charges are going out of the country. They have borrowed outside Canada. In 1984, 92 per cent of all federal government borrowings were from Canadians: Canadian banks, lending institutions and Canadians themselves.
That has dropped off dramatically. That is one of the things that is wrong with this government's policy. It is not borrowing the money from Canadians who want to reinvest in Canada. It is borrowing it offshore and the interest is all going out of the country. Is it any wonder we are in deep trouble? It is going out of the country. It is not benefiting Canadians. It is not giving them a chance to invest in their own country.
That is why I say that with positive programs we can rekindle a sense of pride in being Canadian and rebuild this country. We have done it before after both world wars and we will do it again. Just watch us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the April 26 budget, but above all I would like to send a message to my constituents in Hochelaga- Maisonneuve.
First of all, there will be no tax increases.
I would like to go on to the measures announced in the budget and provide some background as well. There will be no new taxes, less government borrowing, lower taxes, more jobs and more choices for the future. That is what
The Budget
people want and that is the direction in which this government is going.
Spending cuts, together with other measures in this budget and combined with the cutbacks announced in the December 1992 statement, will yield savings of $3.8 billion in 1993-94, rising to $7.9 billion in 1997-98. Over the five-year period the total savings will be more than $30.7 billion.
Between 1993-94 and 1997-98 the average annual growth of program spending will be maintained at 1.7 per cent. This means that, allowing for inflation, there will be zero real growth in program spending.
Reducing the deficit means less government borrowing, lower interest rates and lower taxes, all of which will stimulate economic growth and job creation.
The budget reinforces the action taken in the February 1992 budget and the December 1992 statement, both containing measures aimed at supporting economic recovery.
Specific measures include a one-year exemption from unemployment insurance premiums for new employees of small businesses; a 10 per cent investment tax credit for small businesses; an increase in the loan limit under the Small Businesses Loans Act to $250,000, and a two-year extension of the Small Business Financing Program.
Cuts in personal income taxes and enriching and restructuring the child benefit system will inject $1.7 billion into the economy this year alone. However, we are not the only ones facing financial challenges. These are difficult times and many countries are carrying a heavy load. In fact most are introducing spending cuts similar to our own.
Measures to promote job creation are also included in this budget, which reinforces the measures introduced in the February 1992 budget and the December 1992 economic and fiscal statement by focusing on a sound monetary and fiscal policy, streamlining government spending, upgrading the skills of Canadians and encouraging the private sector to expand and create jobs.
It is essential to restore the financial health of the private sector and thus restore its confidence and facilitate the investment that is essential to economic growth and job creation.

April 28, 1993
The Budget
The home buyers' plan helps Canadians buy or build homes using funds from their RRSPs, and last year
148,000	Canadians took advantage of this plan.
The government has made accommodation more affordable for Canadians, thanks to lower interest rates, the possibility of using RRSP funds for the initial downpayment on a home, and the availability of 95 per cent mortgage insurance for first home buyers.
The federal government, operating through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, will no longer fund housing through 35-year subsidy commitments which impose most of the costs on future taxpayers.
However CMHC will look at ways to increase efficiencies in the financing and delivery of its programs and resulting savings will be reinvested in social housing to maintain existing housing stock in good repair and provide some scope for new commitments. Increased efficiencies will be obtained as a result of direct funding.
CMHC will maintain its current funding level of about $2 billion a year. Similarly, special purpose funding for shelters for victims of family violence, the National Strategy for the Integration of Persons with Disabilities and for native housing on reserves will continue.
Considering the overriding need to restrain spending increases and control the deficit and the national debt, the federal government cannot afford to let new social housing commitments accumulate as it did in the past.
The government, through the Canada Housing and Mortgage Corporation, will be able to maintain its housing stock by spending $2 billion annually and thus meet the needs of 650,000 low income families seeking accommodation. Quebec's subsidy share will remain more or less the same, at $685 million annually. Furthermore, a safety net including the cost of shelter for the indigent will still be provided under the Canada Assistance Plan.
To help control unemployment insurance costs and protect the integrity of the unemployment insurance account the average benefit rate will be maintained at 57 per cent of average weekly insurable earnings after 1995.
For the sake of comparison, in the United States the benefit rate is 50 per cent for a period of six months, while in Japan the rate is 48 per cent for a maximum of 7 months. Canada, with its rate of 57 per cent for a maximum of 12 months compares very favourably in this respect.
In the December 1992 statement we announced that funding for regional development would be reduced by 10 per cent for both 1993-94 and 1994-95.
As a result of measures introduced in the present budget, funding will be reduced by a further $90 million in 1993-94 up to a total of $415 million in 1997-98.
As for repayable contributions, by 1997-98 regional development funding will be reduced by $100 million per year, based on the pool of funds expected as a result of the contribution repayment policy announced in the 1990 budget.
I see you are signalling, Mr. Speaker, but I have not quite finished.
